title: ELA: End-to-End Latent Action Policy Learning from Video Demonstrations
summary: Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/

Additional materials can be found on: end2end-latent-action.github.io Introduction Data scarcity remains a fundamental bottleneck for robot imitation learning, because collecting large-scale datasets~ o2024open, khazatsky2024droid with robot action labels is expensive and often infeasible. In contrast, video demonstrations, including human videos and unlabeled robot trajectories, are significantly easier to obtain at scale. This contrast motivates imitation learning approaches that learn directly from video data without requiring action labels. Latent action modeling~ schmidt2024learning, ye2025latent has recently emerged as a promising direction for leveraging such data. These methods infer action-relevant structure from video demonstrations and use it as the supervision target for policy learning, removing the need for explicit action supervision. This property makes latent action learning particularly promising for leveraging large-scale video data for imitation learning. However, while effective as an abstract representation, existing approaches do not explicitly optimize the latent action space for downstream control. We identify two key properties that a latent action space should satisfy for effective policy learning: modelability, meaning latent actions can be reliably inferred from observations for policy learning, and decodability, meaning they can be faithfully mapped into executable continuous robot actions. Existing methods~ ye2025latent, kim2025uniskill, bu2025univla, routray2025vipra typically adopt a two-stage pipeline, where latent actions are first learned from image pairs and then used as fixed targets for a downstream policy. This decoupling leads to a latent space that is not explicitly shaped for either reliable inference from observations or accurate execution, potentially resulting in latent actions that are difficult to predict or decode. In this work, we study whether latent actions can instead serve as a unified interface for imitation learning that is jointly optimized for both modelability and decodability. To that end, this paper introduces the framework shown in Figure~ fig: teaser , in which latent actions act as both the supervision signal for policy learning and the interface for action execution. By jointly optimizing the latent space with respect to both policy learning and action decoding, our method learns latent actions that can effectively leverage action-free video data while requiring relatively little action-labeled data for decoding into continuous robot actions. learns from a mixture of action-labeled and action-free demonstrations by jointly training three components: a Latent Action Model, a Latent Action Policy, and an Action Decoder. The Latent Action Model infers a latent action responsible for each state transition, which are then used as supervision for the Latent Action Policy. This approach enables policy learning directly from video data without modifying the underlying policy architecture or objective, while ensuring modelability by shaping a latent space such that latent actions corresponding to demonstrations are predictable. The Action Decoder maps latent actions into continuous robot control commands, ensuring decodability. To prevent latent action collapse during joint training, we further introduce a representation alignment objective that stabilizes the latent space. Overall, enables imitation learning from video demonstrations by learning a latent action space that is explicitly optimized for both modelability and decodability. It effectively leverages video data and outperforms other latent action baselines across simulated and real-world benchmarks. Moreover, it can be integrated into existing imitation learning approaches without modifying policy architectures or training objectives, using a lightweight Action Decoder that adds a fixed 4M-parameter overhead independent of policy size. Related Work Learning from video demonstrations~ torabi2018behavioral enables robots to acquire skills without requiring action labels, alleviating the data scarcity bottleneck in robot imitation learning. Prior works extracts action-relevant information from videos through intermediate representations such as hand poses~ haldar2025point, hong2025hand , object poses~ hsu2025spot, su2025motion , and point tracks~ wen2023any, collins2025amplify . These methods typically rely on external vision systems, including hand pose predictors~ chen2025large and object pose estimators~ patel2025robotic , and often require carefully designed architectures tailored to specific representations. Another line of work, world action models (WAM)~ zhu2025unified, li2025unified, pai2025mimic , leverages video data through world modeling objectives such as next-frame prediction. While effective for learning visual dynamics, these approaches generally do not recover action representations that can directly supervise policy learning. Latent action modeling~ schmidt2024learning, ye2025latent instead learns inverse dynamics models (IDMs) that infer latent actions from video, enabling training on diverse data sources including human videos~ yang2025egovla and robot datasets~ khazatsky2024droid . However, latent actions are often too abstract for direct low-level control and are mainly used for policy pretraining~ ye2025latent, kim2025uniskill, bu2025univla, routray2025vipra . Recent methods~ liang2025clam, chen2025villa, zhang2026clap incorporate proprioception and action supervision, but the separate training of the IDM and policy often leads to sub-optimal performance. In contrast, jointly learns the inverse dynamics model and control policy, enabling direct end-to-end policy learning from action-labeled and action-free demonstrations. title: $\mathcal{C}^\infty$ Smooth Trajectory Planning with Application to Soft Robots
summary: High motion performance and avoiding structural vibrations rely on smooth trajectory planning. The smoothness requirement depends on the robot's complexity in terms of the number of degrees of freedom and system order due to the flexibility of the joints and links. For industrial robots, the smoothness requirements have been determined and subsequently taken into account. Although unknown for soft continuum robots, the exact smoothness requirement can potentially be much larger than previously considered ones such as $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^4}$ for collaborative robots and $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^5}$ for quadcopter drones. To address this gap, we introduce a $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^\infty}$-smooth trajectory generator that respects defined kinematic limits and generates infinitely differentiable trajectories. The generated path addresses and generalizes to all smoothness requirements, where a transition between sequential states is needed. Therefore, all trajectories have continuous velocity, acceleration, jerk, snap, crackle, pop, etc. Of particular interest is the case of null boundary conditions, i.e., all derivatives at the start and end of the trajectory are equal to zero. We verified and evaluated our proposed approach in simulations and on hardware.

To achieve this, a trajectory generator is used to provide suitable intermediate values in actuation space, task space, or any intermediate space, e.g., joint space or arc space. The smoothness of those generated trajectories is important as non-smooth trajectories may cause vibrations due to the capability of exciting the eigenmodes of the mechanical system. That is why, as shown by De Luca Book DeLucaBook_HOR_2016 , the smoothness requirement for a robot with flexible elements can, e.g., go as high as twice the number of flexible joints and links, respectively. Following the widely assumed approach that, in the limit, a hyper-redundant robot is a soft continuum robot, a soft continuum robot has infinitely many flexible elements. Therefore, according to different authors from Chirikjian Burdick ChirikjianBurdick_ICRA_1990 to Burgner-Kahrs et al. Burgner-KahrsRuckerChoset_TRO_2015 , those robots have infinite degrees of freedom. Consequently, soft continuum robots require infinitely differentiable smooth trajectories, i.e., smooth trajectories. In general, smooth trajectories are desirable because they avoid the above-mentioned structural oscillations, help increase accuracy in tracking the end effector, and can reduce energy consumption in tracking tasks. Therefore, the generation of trajectories is well covered by standard robotics textbooks, e.g., Craig Craig_book_2005 , and by a dedicated textbook BiagiottiMelchiorri_book_2008 on this subject. However, most of the trajectories in the literature are designed for industrial robots and show smoothness or even less. Some trajectory generators, e.g., GrassmannJohannsmeierHaddadin_IROS_2018 , designed for collaborative robots with mechanical flexibility, such as FR3 HaddadinHaddadin_et_al_RAM_2022 and DLR LWR-III Albu-SchaefferHirzinger_et_al_IRIJ_2007 , exist. Those smooth trajectories have continuously differentiable jerk. Unfortunately, in soft continuum robotics, most authors do not specify the smoothness of the trajectory used. If any reference trajectory is utilized, linear interpolation between configurations is the current norm. For quasi-static motions, as required for safety in medical robots DupontRucker_et_al_PROC_2022 , soft continuum robots are often position-controlled, where the intermediate states are not interpolated. Furthermore, survey and review articles, e.g., RobinsonDavies_ICRA_1999,Burgner-KahrsRuckerChoset_TRO_2015,ChikhaouiBurgner-Kahrs_ACTUATOR_2018,RussoAxinte_et_al_AIS_2023,LilgeBurgner-Kahrs_et_al_TRO_2024 , neither discuss nor identify trajectory generation as a potential open challenge. We believe that this represents an overlooked potential to improve the performance of downstream methods with low implementation effort. When generating a trajectory, the boundaries at the beginning and the end of the trajectory need to match the previous and subsequent trajectory boundaries, respectively. title: Correct Robots Before They Make Mistakes: Proactive Human-in-the-Loop Intervention via Preference Learning
summary: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.

Introduction sec:introduction Robot policies, including visuomotor policies and vision-language-action (VLA) models, have shown strong performance on a broad range of manipulation tasks. However, policies trained from offline demonstrations may still encounter states that are beyond the coverage of their training data. In such situations, the policy may produce undesirable motions or fail to complete the task. Improving performance in such cases requires additional task-specific data. Human-in-the-loop imitation learning addresses this gap by collecting corrective data during policy rollouts. During these rollouts, the policy may visit states that are absent from, or underrepresented in the offline demonstrations. Most existing human-in-the-loop methods collect correction data reactively. In reactive correction, the operator decides whether to intervene based on the robot's currently observed execution, without a preview of the policy's predicted future motion. It is straightforward to deploy and allows corrective data to be collected during policy rollouts. The resulting recovery actions can also be valuable when the robot must recover from an error and retry a task~ Hu2025RaC . This approach has enabled effective policy refinement through interactive data aggregation, remote teleoperation, and corrective residual control~ hg-dagger,Mandlekar2020RemoteTeleop,xu2025crdagger . When reactive corrections begin after an error has occurred, they include recovery actions in addition to actions that advance the task. The proportion of reactive correction data in the dataset can affect how often recovery motions appear in the policy output. A higher proportion increases the likelihood of producing recovery motions even when no recovery is needed. These limitations motivate proactive correction, in which the operator reviews the policy's proposed motion and provides corrections before an anticipated error occurs. By visualizing the policy's predicted future motion, proactive correction enables the operator to identify and correct potential errors before the robot enters safety-critical states. This predictive preview reduces the operator's cognitive burden of continuously anticipating the policy's behavior. It can also reduce the need for repeated reactive corrections as an error unfolds. Although proactive correction shows considerable promise, it has received limited attention. Existing work has considered simulated tasks in autonomous driving and robotic manipulation~ Cai2025PPL , while its application to complex physical robot manipulation remains unexplored. Extending proactive correction to such tasks requires an interface that allows the operator to intuitively assess the robot's proposed three-dimensional motion before an anticipated error occurs. Although a screen-based preview can overlay this motion on a camera view, judging its depth and spatial orientation from a two-dimensional display can be difficult. To address this challenge, we propose PHIL, a proactive human-in-the-loop imitation learning framework that uses an Extended Reality (XR) interface to visualize proposed policy action chunks in the physical workspace. Each action chunk is converted into a sequence of three-dimensional end-effector poses and spatially registered with the physical workspace. The operator can therefore inspect upcoming motion in three dimensions within its execution context while the robot executes the current action chunk. When the preview indicates that the proposed motion may lead to an error, the operator takes control and provides corrections before the anticipated undesirable action occurs. During the takeover, PHIL continues to query the policy at the unchanged query schedule and display updated action chunks in the XR headset. PHIL constructs contrastive pairs from the displayed policy action chunks and the corresponding executed corrective robot trajectories. For each retained policy query during intervention, the displayed action chunk is recorded as rejected, denoted by \(A_t^-\). The next \(H\) executed robot actions starting at that query form the corresponding corrective action chunk \(A_t^+\), which may include policy-controlled actions after release. Both action chunks in each pair start from the same physical state. When the operator judges the most recently displayed action chunk to be acceptable, they release control and the robot returns to policy control. After data collection, PHIL uses the contrastive pairs to fine-tune the policy, encouraging it to favor executed corrective action chunks \(A_t^+\) over rejected policy action chunks \(A_t^-\) from the same physical state. We evaluate PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks, with experiments covering both diffusion and pretrained VLA policies. Compared with HG-DAgger, PHIL increases the average success rate from 44.0 to 70.3 for the diffusion policy and from 57.8 to 76.9 for X-VLA. Proactive correction data reduce unnecessary recovery behaviors approximately tenfold compared with reactive correction data. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: We introduce PHIL, a proactive human-in-the-loop framework that leverages XR to visualize proposed robot motions in the physical workspace, enabling human corrections before anticipated errors occur. We extract rejected--corrected action-chunk pairs anchored at the same physical state during human takeover and use them for preference-based post-training to favor executed corrective trajectories over rejected policy actions. We evaluate PHIL on real-world manipulation tasks with diffusion and pretrained VLA policies, demonstrating improved task success and showing that proactive correction data reduce unnecessary recovery behaviors. Related Work Human-in-the-Loop Robot Learning Prior human-in-the-loop robot learning methods collect additional training data through human takeovers during policy rollouts, using assistance requests and control switching to reduce intervention burden~ hg-dagger,hoque2022thriftydagger,hoque2021lazydagger,Hoque2024IntervenGen . Recent methods extend interactive learning to generative visuomotor and vision-language-action policies through uncertainty-guided intervention, corrective post-training, and online adaptation~ He2025Uncertainty,Han2025DexHiL,Murray2026FlowDAgger,Welte2026FlowCorrect . These methods address supervision allocation and policy learning. PHIL informs intervention decisions through an XR preview of proposed motion in the physical workspace, enabling takeover before anticipated errors. Corrective Imitation Learning Corrective imitation learning mitigates distribution shift in behavior cloning by collecting supervision at states encountered during policy rollouts~ ross2011reduction . For action-chunking visuomotor policies, which predict short action sequences~ reuss2023goal , an unsuitable motion may be partly executed before its consequences become apparent to the operator. PPL visualizes predicted future trajectories to support proactive intervention and propagates intervention-derived preferences to predicted future states~ Cai2025PPL . SDP uses paired undesired and corrective action chunks to construct sets of desired actions for diffusion-policy training~ Li2026SDP . PHIL uses proactive correction for preference-based post-training of diffusion and pretrained VLA policies in real-world manipulation. During human takeover, it pairs each retained, unexecuted policy prediction with the subsequent executed corrective action chunk from the same physical state and spanning the same temporal horizon. Extended Reality for Robotics Extended Reality (XR) supports spatial visualization and three-dimensional interaction for robot learning. AR-based systems enable robot-free demonstration collection~ ar2-d2-pmlr-v229-duan23a,eve and provide visual feedback for collecting demonstrations~ arcade,chen2024arcap,jiang2024comprehensive . Other interfaces support immersive teleoperation and demonstration collection~ holodex,opentelevision , interactive skill maintenance~ arclfd , and robot interaction across simulated and physical environments~ jiang2025iris . VR-DAgger further combines immersive interaction with uncertainty-guided selection and correction of policy rollout segments~ Zurbrugg2026VRDagger . PHIL renders the future end-effector trajectory implied by a policy action chunk in registration with the physical workspace, allowing the operator to assess upcoming motion relative to the robot and surrounding objects during execution and intervene proactively. Method sec:method PHIL post-trains an action-chunking robot policy using proactive corrections collected before an anticipated undesirable action occurs. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:proactive_correction , the operator inspects the policy's predicted future motion during execution. If an error is anticipated, the operator takes control of the robot to provide corrective actions. The policy continues to generate predictions on its fixed query schedule during the takeover. Retained predictions are paired with subsequent executed corrective action chunks from the same query state and used for preference-based post-training. Introduction Olfaction, the sense of smell, enables organisms to perceive the chemical state of their surroundings through airborne cues, allowing them to detect spoiled food, burning materials, hazardous gases, and other signals that may be invisible or difficult to distinguish visually. Accordingly, olfaction has attracted substantial interest across biology, cognitive science, and chemistry~ chem, molecular, central, stevenson2013olfactory , where prior work has examined how airborne chemicals are sensed, neurally and perceptually represented, and related to molecular structure. Despite its importance, machine olfaction remains largely underexplored compared to vision, audition, and touch. Existing learning-based work has mainly focused on semantic odor perception sanchezlengeling2019machinelearningscentlearning, doi:10.1126/science.ade4401, ozguroglu2025newyorksmellslarge, feng2025smellnetlargescaledatasetrealworld,kim2026see , such as odor classification and representation learning. However, odor is not only semantic, but also inherently spatial. Airborne chemicals are emitted from localized sources and transported by airflow, diffusion, and mixing, forming concentration fields that vary over space and time. In many real-world scenarios, the goal is therefore not merely to recognize an odor, but to infer its source: identifying an invisible gas leak before it accumulates, locating an early-stage fire before visible smoke appears, or tracing chemical cues toward concealed substances such as explosives or narcotics. While pre-installed gas detectors can trigger safety alarms, their fixed locations provide only sparse measurements and are not designed for active source seeking. Mobile embodied agents offer a natural way to address this gap. By moving through an environment, they can actively sample chemical concentrations over time to infer where an odor originates. Yet most prior work on embodied navigation has focused on visual, auditory, and language-guided perception~ anderson2018vision, chen2020soundspaces, chen2023soundspaces20simulationplatform, listenact , with little attention to olfactory sensing. This limits agents in safety-critical scenarios where gas leaks, smoke, or hazardous chemical sources may be invisible, occluded, or difficult to localize visually. Olfactory navigation is also challenging: odor measurements provide only local, noisy evidence of a dynamic concentration field, with weak or patchy readings, misleading local peaks, and directional cues that may emerge only over time. Reliable navigation therefore requires integrating odor measurements over time while using vision to traverse the 3D environment. We formalize this challenge as visual-olfactory embodied navigation, where an agent uses visual observations and gas sensor measurements to navigate toward an odor source in a 3D environment. Training and benchmarking visual-olfactory embodied agents directly in the real world remains challenging. Odor transport is highly sensitive to airflow, temperature, scene geometry, source properties, and ventilation, making odor dynamics hard to reproduce for controlled algorithmic comparison. Prior work often relies on small-scale or geometrically simplified environments s24072309, MAHMUD2025104915, liu2026scensoryrealtimeroboticolfactory , which are difficult to scale to visually and geometrically complex indoor spaces. Advancing visual-olfactory embodied navigation therefore requires a simulation framework with physically grounded odor dynamics, a well-defined task, and standardized evaluation protocols in realistic 3D scenes. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based embodied simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces uses Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) McGrattan2004 to simulate 3D odor transport and dispersion, and integrates the resulting odor fields into Habitat-Sim habitat19iccv environments built from Replica replica19arxiv and Matterport3D Matterport3D scenes. The benchmark covers two representative real-world source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas leak localization, modeled using propane (C H ), a dense gas that settles and spreads near the floor; and early-stage fire localization via combustion-generated carbon dioxide (CO ), modeled as a methanol pool fire where heat-driven buoyancy transports gas upward. Together, these scenarios capture distinct physical regimes of odor transport and provide standardized protocols for evaluating odor-guided navigation. To support this new task, we develop an initial learning-based visual-olfactory navigation policy that combines visual observations, olfactory measurements, and pose history with recurrent memory for action prediction. Experiments show that the policy achieves competitive performance against diverse baselines, highlighting the value of multimodal perception and spatio-temporal modeling for odor-guided navigation. Together, OdorSpaces provides a physics-based simulation platform, a standardized benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation, and a reference baseline for future research on embodied agents with smell sensing. Related Work Machine Olfaction. Odor has long been studied as a chemical and perceptual signal in biology, cognitive science, and chemistry~ chem, molecular, central, stevenson2013olfactory . Machine olfaction extends this idea to computational systems that sense and interpret odors from chemical measurements, including electronic noses, gas-sensors, and odor recognition systems~ machineolfaction, nose, nosereview . Recent work has mainly focused on semantic odor understanding, such as modeling structure-to-odor-perception relationships~ sanchezlengeling2019machinelearningscentlearning, doi:10.1126/science.ade4401 , recognizing odor categories from sensor measurements, and learning multimodal odor representations with visual or chemical information~ ozguroglu2025newyorksmellslarge, feng2025smellnetlargescaledatasetrealworld,kim2026see . These works study what an odor is or how it can be represented, whereas OdorSpaces studies odor as a spatial and temporal signal for embodied navigation. Odor Source Localization. Odor source localization (OSL) studies how agents locate odor sources from local chemical measurements. Classical formulations decompose OSL into plume finding, plume tracking, and source declaration~ s24072309, liu2026scensoryrealtimeroboticolfactory, chen2019odor . Existing methods include gradient-based search~ russell1995robotic,alt1980biased,jabeen2023robot , bio-inspired tracking~ ishida1994study,nakata2024olfactory,shigaki2023robust,fukui2025advanced,lochmatter2010bio , probabilistic or map-based estimation~ vergassola2007infotaxis,rahbar2019design,li2011odor,hutchinson2018unmanned , and multi-robot search~ marques2006particle,ferri2007explorative,meng2011collective,zhang2015localizing,jain2018odor,gaurav2020single , and recent learning-based systems use deep RL, recurrent policies, VOC sensor arrays, or vision-language models for odor-guided search~ liu2026scensoryrealtimeroboticolfactory,loisy2023deep,10473576,hassan2024integrating . While these methods demonstrate the promise of odor-guided navigation, they are often evaluated under simplified plume dynamics, limited scene geometry, and single controlled testbeds. In contrast, OdorSpaces provides a standardized embodied navigation benchmark in photorealistic indoor environments with physics-based 3D odor fields. Multimodal Embodied Navigation. Embodied AI has benefited from 3D simulators and benchmarks for navigation, interaction, and policy learning, including Habitat-Sim~ habitat19iccv , AI2-THOR~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1712-05474 , MINOS~ savva2017minosmultimodalindoorsimulator , and VirtualHome~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1806-07011 . Beyond vision-only navigation~ wijmans2019ddppo, chaplot2020object , multimodal embodied navigation studies how agents use additional sensory cues to perceive and act in 3D environments~ anderson2018vision, chen2020soundspaces, chen2023soundspaces20simulationplatform, listenact, avlen, gao2023sonicverse . Audio-visual navigation is a representative example, with prior work introducing spatial audio simulation and navigation tasks that use sound as a spatial or semantic cue~ chen2020soundspaces,chen2023soundspaces20simulationplatform,listenact,chen2021semanticaudiovisualnavigation,chen2021learningsetwaypointsaudiovisual . OdorSpaces studies a complementary setting: visual-olfactory embodied navigation. Unlike audio, odor is sensed through local gas measurements of a time-varying concentration field shaped by transport, dispersion, accumulation, and scene geometry. As a result, odor cues can be weak, intermittent, and history-dependent, making odor-guided navigation an active sensing problem that requires integrating visual context, gas measurements, and past observations. title: Learning Object-Centric Motion Priors from Human for Robotic Dexterous Manipulation
comment: Accepted as an oral paper at AAAI 2026 (Website: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38892)
summary: Manipulating diverse objects with multi-fingered dexterous hands is challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex dynamics. Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets provide rich knowledge about task information and embodied interactions. Instead of solely imitating the human demonstrations, our method learns to holistically predict future hand-object states by leveraging these datasets. The predicted future states of the object can serve as a general-purpose reward term for reinforcement learning, reducing reliance on task-specific reward engineering and enhancing generalization across tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world. Our approach outperforms existing SOTA methods in both success rate and generalizability on novel objects. Furthermore, we validate the cross-embodiment compatibility of our methods by successfully deploying the skills on different robot hands.

Previous methods, such as model-based trajectory optimization pang2023global, jin2024complementarity , struggle with these dynamic complexities. Meanwhile, model-free reinforcement learning (RL) rajeswaran2017learning, gupta2016learning, akkaya2019solving, chen2023visual, wang2024lessons is often inefficient, demanding extensive exploration and task-specific reward engineering. While imitation learning from robot data chi2023diffusion presents a viable solution, the required large-scale data collection is frequently impractical for research labs wang2024dexcap, black2410pi0 . In contrast, the vast amount of available human data, which implicitly encodes rich manipulation experience, offers a promising and scalable alternative for learning dexterous manipulation. What should we learn from the human demonstration? To answer this, let's look at how humans learn. Children learn to interact with the physical world using the following two-stage learning paradigm. The first stage involves forming an abstract task concept through watching others play. In the second stage, this conceptual knowledge is grounded and refined through physical experimentation by themselves, facilitating the development of operational competence. Similarly, prior literature~ qin2022dexmv,chen2024vividex,shi2025learning, chen2024object, li2025maniptrans investigates a similar two-stage pipeline for learning dexterous manipulation skills. Most of them either focus solely on imitating human motions or designing task-specific rewards, then testing on only one task, which makes it hard to draw a general conclusion from that. Some of these works overlook an important fact: while humans are manipulating objects, they are also subconsciously predicting the future state changes of the objects. This ability to predict the future state of objects not only helps humans understand tasks but also enables them to perform more general operations on different tasks. Inspired by that, our observation is that considering human-object as a whole and learning human manipulation priors from hand-object interactions provides more general and efficient task-level guidance for the second-stage low-level policy learning. Instead of using human-designed task-specific rewards like lifting rewards in previous work~ chen2024vividex, shi2025learning , we believe that human-object interaction priors encourage robots to manipulate the object in the way described in the dataset, which is task-agnostic to different tasks. Specifically, we propose a pipeline to auto-regressively predict future hand-object states holistically. And we use the predicted hand and object states to guide the low-level policy learning in different tasks without task-specific reward design in low-level reinforcement learning in a physical simulation. Then we perform zero-shot sim-to-real skill transfer to the real-world robots. Our contributions are as follows: We propose an efficient learning framework to utilize human-object interaction priors for robot skill learning, without the need for real-robot data. Predicting hand-object priors holistically and properly utilizing the predicted object states can not only facilitate reinforcement learning by alleviating the heavy reliance on task-specific reward design, but also enable our pipeline to be more general to various task settings. We conducted extensive real-robot experiments on various tasks, embodiments, and object settings, outperforming existing SOTA methods in all three challenging tasks. Related Work Dexterous Manipulation Dexterous manipulation is complicated by the high dimensionality of the end effector. This complexity poses a problem for traditional trajectory optimization techniques rus1999hand, mordatch2012contact, wu2022learning , as they require precise dynamic models that are impractical for real-world applications. Learning-based methods address this by learning an observation-to-action policy directly from data, but they introduce new challenges. Reinforcement learning approaches qi2023general, yuan2024robot, wang2024lessons can be sample-inefficient and depend on meticulous reward engineering. On the other hand, imitation learning methods bain1995framework, chi2023diffusion , which use data from teleoperation qin2023anyteleop, wang2024dexcap , are often constrained by the expense of data collection and the quality of the expert demonstrations. Vision-Language-Action methods~ pan2024vision, zhong2025dexgraspvla aim at utilizing pretrained language models to boost the network performance, while only demonstrating tasks not harder than pick-and-place. Grasp synthesis methods~ ye2025dex1b,wan2023unidexgrasp++ are mainly tested in simulation, and the potential in more challenging tasks beyond pick-and-place is not fully investigated. Our methods combine the merits of using human data and scaled-up simulation, enabling real-robot dexterous manipulation with high success rates. Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Human Internet human video data contains abundant information about human experiences. Previous research mendonca2023structured, ma2022vip, nair2022r3m seeks to learn general visual representations from internet-scale human video data to guide robot learning. However, those methods only showcase results on a 1-DoF robot gripper since the features trained on 2D human videos lack the 3D information necessary for learning high-dimensional skills like dexterous manipulation. Different from internet video human data, human-object interaction (HOI) data chao2021dexycb, fan2023arctic, liu2022hoi4d are usually collected by multi-view RGBD cameras, with extracted and labeled 3D human pose estimations and 6-DoF object pose estimations, which contain abundant 3D information necessary for learning dexterous manipulation. Given the 3D motions of the human hand, an intuitive idea is to directly transfer human motions to robot actions. qin2023anyteleop proposed a retargeting system based on inverse kinematics to map the human hand motions to robot hand states and actions. qin2022dexmv,liu2025dextrack further prove that the retargeted trajectories can be used to train imitation learning policies in different tasks. Following them, chen2024vividex, zhou2024learning, shi2025learning apply trajectory augmentation and train a state-based policy based on that. Different from direct mapping, chen2024object proposes to train a human motion prediction network given a target object trajectory, then augment and refine it in physical simulation using Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, defining target object trajectories in open world requires extra efforts. li2025maniptrans train a 2-stage process imitating human, but their input is fixed object initial poses with object pose randomization as 0, constraining open-world applications. To address this, zhao2024dexh2r introduces human-in-the-loop adjustments in generating reference trajectories, but it requires human labor. singh2024hand requires real-world robot demonstrations or RL to finetune the policy. Most of them focus on a single task and can hardly generalize to novel object configurations. We demonstrate our applicability in various challenging tasks under different object configurations. title: 3D Pose Estimation in Projection Space via Pixel-level Visible Light Communication
summary: Projector-based augmented reality enables natural interaction between users and devices by overlaying digital information onto the physical world through projected imagery. A key technical requirement of such systems is accurate positional alignment between the projector and the devices. Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC) achieves this alignment without external sensing infrastructure by embedding invisible spatial codes into each projected pixel through high-speed brightness modulation that preserves image quality. However, the information that PVLC transmits is inherently planar. PVLC has therefore been limited to devices moving on a flat surface and cannot estimate the 3D pose of devices in three-dimensional space, such as aerial robots. To extend PVLC-based pose estimation to three dimensions, we formulate it as a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem. The 2D pixel positions that four coplanar photosensors on the device receive via PVLC serve as the image points, and their known 3D layout provides the object points. Experiments show that the proposed system estimates 3D pose with a latency of approximately 8~ms and a 3D position RMSE of 19.2~mm after Kalman filtering. These results confirm the first realization of real-time 3D pose estimation coordinated with high-quality projected image content without external sensing infrastructure.

Among them, projector-based AR, also known as Spatial Augmented Reality (SAR)~ bimber2005spatial , overlays information directly onto real space with projected images. Because users do not need to wear special devices such as head-mounted displays, SAR enables more natural interaction. This technology has already produced many promising applications, including efficient teaching operations for industrial robots~ 10.1145/3371382.3378266, 10.1145/3351180.3351204 , tabletop interfaces using mobile robots~ Rosenfeld2004-gd, 10.1145/3301275.3302326, 10.1145/3332165.3347911 , and interactive art~ Darbar2019-kg . To seamlessly coordinate device behavior with projected image content, the system must obtain the position of the device relative to the projector with high accuracy. Achieving such accuracy typically requires external sensing equipment such as cameras~ 9107397 or motion capture systems~ furniss2000motion , as well as geometric calibration between the projector and these sensors~ lee2004automatic . This requirement increases setup complexity and limits practical deployment. Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC)~ kitamura2007KJ00007499118 , a projector-based visible light communication technique, has been proposed to address these challenges. PVLC embeds invisible position codes into each pixel of the projected image through high-speed brightness modulation. A photosensor on the device decodes the pixel coordinate at its location to obtain its own position within the image. Because no external sensors or projector-sensor calibration is required, and because the embedded information is invisible to the human eye, PVLC enables device localization alongside high-quality projected content. However, the projected image is inherently planar, and the position that a device obtains from it is limited to two dimensions. PVLC has therefore been applied only to devices moving on a plane, such as ground robots~ Hiraki2018-ri , and cannot support devices that operate in three-dimensional space, such as aerial robots. (topskip=0pt, botskip=0pt, midskip=0pt)[width=0.99 ] figures/concept.png Conceptual overview of the proposed 3D pose estimation system using Pixel-level Visible Light Communication (PVLC). The projector embeds invisible position codes into each pixel. Multiple photosensors on the device decode their 2D pixel coordinates, which are combined with the projector's intrinsic parameters and the known 3D sensor geometry, and fed into a PnP solver to estimate the device's 3D pose. fig:concept To overcome this limitation, we extend PVLC-based localization from two dimensions to three by formulating it as a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem~ Fischler1981-ce . Fig.~ fig:concept shows an overview of the proposed method. The PnP problem is widely used for camera-based pose estimation. In our formulation, the 2D pixel coordinates that multiple photosensors on the device decode via PVLC serve as the image points, and their known 3D layout provides the object points. Solving this problem gives the 3D pose of the device with respect to the projector. This approach enables 3D device control in coordination with high-quality projected images without projector-sensor calibration and opens up applications such as aerial robot navigation. We conduct three experiments to validate the proposed method: (1) evaluation of pose estimation accuracy under different movement speeds and photosensor layout sizes, with a camera-based AR marker method as a baseline, (2) comparison of multiple PnP solvers to identify the most suitable one for the system, and (3) investigation of the effectiveness of Kalman filter-based smoothing on estimation accuracy. The results demonstrate that the system achieves centimeter-order position estimation accuracy with a latency of approximately 8~ms. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: The first application of PnP-based 3D pose estimation to PVLC. By solving the PnP problem with the 2D pixel coordinates decoded by multiple photosensors, the method extends PVLC-based localization from 2D to 3D. A content display region and a 3D pose tracking region that both cover the entire projection area at the same time. Because PVLC embeds the position codes into every pixel of the displayed content, the tracking region coincides with the content display region. Neither a dedicated tracking region nor an external sensor is required. Evaluation on a device moving at speeds from 50 to 400~mm/s. By combining the pose estimation with a Kalman filter, the method achieved a 3D position RMSE of 19.2~mm over all trajectories and movement speeds with the 80~mm photosensor layout. Related Work sec:related_work Pose estimation using projected light determines the position and orientation of a target device with light sources fixed in the environment. This approach is widely used for high-precision indoor localization. These methods can be broadly classified into two categories: methods that observe light projected onto a device with external cameras, and methods that employ visible light communication. Pose Estimation Method Using Cameras In external-camera-based methods~ furniss2000motion,optitrack , markers composed of retroreflective materials are attached to the device, and its pose is estimated by observing the markers with multiple cameras. This approach acquires the position of an object simply by attaching compact markers to it. It has therefore been widely adopted in human motion capture, which requires accurate measurement of numerous joint positions~ davis1991gait,CHARLTON2004213 . Structured-light methods project specific patterns, such as grids and dots, from a light source. They use the projected patterns as feature points and thus acquire positions without markers~ Yuichi_TAMURA2012,6909541,6909459 . Time-of-flight (ToF) cameras have also been used to estimate the pose of markerless targets from depth point clouds~ park2025tof . These camera-based methods are well-established approaches for device pose estimation. However, to create applications that coordinate projected content with device movement, high-accuracy calibration between the observing camera and the projection display is required. In addition, the device must receive its position from the external camera system over a separate communication channel. This communication introduces non-negligible latency into the position update. Pose Estimation Method Using Visible Light Communication Visible light communication (VLC) has been actively studied for indoor positioning, and a wide range of algorithms have been proposed~ Luo2017-vlc-survey . Projector-based VLC methods transmit position information through high-speed blinking of projector light, and photosensors on the device receive it for pose estimation. Various techniques have been proposed, including methods that project multiple Gray code patterns~ lee2004automatic,10.1145/1095034.1095045,Le_Goc2016-dg,10.1145/1186562.1015738 and M-sequence patterns~ 10.1145/2501988.2502022 , as well as methods that alternately blink dozens of LEDs~ 1565405 . These methods enable high-speed position acquisition, but they degrade the native image quality of the projector by reducing resolution or sacrificing full-color display. This degradation diminishes the user experience in applications that coordinate projected content with device motion. To address these limitations, we focus on PVLC~ kitamura2007KJ00007499118 . PVLC uses the digital micromirror device (DMD) of a projector to rapidly modulate the brightness of the three primary color channels of every pixel in the projected image. This modulation transmits position information while preserving the perceived image quality. PVLC has been applied to various domains, including robot swarm control~ Hiraki2018-ri,Hiraki2019-fn and extension to infrared wavelengths for improved image contrast~ Kamei2019-pilc . However, all existing PVLC-based pose estimation methods remain limited to 2D localization, as the transmitted information inherently encodes only 2D pixel coordinates. While VLC-based 3D localization for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms has been explored using ceiling-mounted LEDs~ Xu2023-uav-vlc , it does not address coordination with projector-displayed content. Spatial interactive applications such as aerial robot navigation require 3D pose estimation with PVLC, but no prior work has addressed this problem. Perspective-n-Point Formulation in Projector Systems In computer vision, the PnP problem~ Fischler1981-ce is a well-established framework for recovering 3D pose from 2D--3D point correspondences. Efficient solvers such as EPnP~ Lepetit2009-yg and the homography decomposition method~ Faugeras1988MotionAS are widely used in camera-based systems. The same formulation appears in projector-based SAR. In this setting, a projector is treated as an inverse camera and registered onto a 3D physical object from 2D--3D correspondences between projector pixels and object points~ raskar2002cartoon . Furthermore, photosensors embedded in the target can acquire such correspondences automatically by receiving the projection patterns presented by the projector~ lee2004automatic,10.1145/1186562.1015738 . Projector-based tracking extends this idea to moving display surfaces~ 10.1145/1095034.1095045 . It is the closest to our problem setting, as it localizes a device using a projector and photosensors mounted on the device. However, the limited refresh rate of conventional projectors requires such tracking to reserve dedicated regions for tracking patterns within the projected image, separate from the displayed content. These regions occupy part of the image without contributing to the content. Because tracking is lost once a photosensor leaves the tracking region, the movement speed of the device is also limited. full_text: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object's location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System~2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a vision-language-action policy (System~1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System~1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13 of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals. Introduction Manipulation can depend on information that is no longer visible: an object's identity before it is covered, the order of a demonstrated sequence, or the number of repetitions already completed. RoboMME~ dai2026robomme tests these dependencies with 16 tasks in four suites: Counting, Permanence, Reference, and Imitation. A common design for such tasks is hierarchical, with a vision-language model (VLM) choosing the next subtask and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy executing it. In our development runs, small high-level VLMs often misread RoboMME's video inputs and issued wrong subtasks, so we use GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026astra as the planner. Calling it before every action chunk, however, is expensive and mostly redundant: a chosen subtask usually remains valid for several chunks, and whether it has finished can be judged from the last few frames. We therefore place a small learned monitor between the planner and the policy. Astra is called at the start of an episode and again only when the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs. In between, the VLA keeps executing the same instruction from fresh observations. We evaluate the full system on RoboMME and report success rates, planner usage, and failure cases. Related work. RoboMME compares symbolic and perceptual memory interfaces~ dai2026robomme . SAM2Act adds a visual memory bank~ fang2025sam2act , MemER retrieves keyframes~ sridhar2026memer , and MEM combines short-horizon video with long-horizon text memory~ torne2026mem . Hierarchical systems such as -VLA use execution memory and test-time reasoning to select subtasks~ cai2026tau . Our system instead sends task-dependent history to an external planner at each call and lets a local monitor decide when to call it. Three-Tier System sec:method Figure~ fig:method (a) shows the three components. Let be the episode instruction, the observation at environment step , and the th grounded subtask. System 2: History and Grounded Planning At each planning event, Astra produces one executable instruction: where is the history passed to the planner. It has three parts: the demonstration video when the task provides one, selected execution frames that may show objects now hidden, and a text progress record that lists issued subtasks and monitor-confirmed subtasks separately. Repeated actions are recorded as separate entries, so their order and count remain available. Each request also includes the current front-camera image and the image at execution start. Astra keeps no state between calls; all history is sent with each request. Which history is sent and which output templates are allowed are configured per task: nine tasks receive the demonstration video and four receive dense execution history (Appendix~ app:implementation ; full prompts in Appendix~ app:prompts ). When a target must be localized, the instruction contains a pixel coordinate in the current image. The output is checked against the templates before it reaches the VLA. System 1: Low-Level Action Execution We use RoboMME's grounded-subgoal policy~ black2025pi05 : where includes camera images and robot state. Each chunk runs 16 environment steps. The same can guide several consecutive chunks, and each chunk is predicted from a new observation, so control remains closed-loop while Astra is idle. System 1.5: Visual Progress Monitoring sec:monitor The monitor is Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct~ qwen3vl , fine-tuned with LoRA on RoboMME demonstrations to predict a binary event for the active subtask: The input has ten images: eight recent front-camera frames taken three steps apart (spanning up to 21 steps), the front image from when the current instruction was issued, and the current wrist image. This reference image is reset whenever an instruction is issued, even if its text repeats an earlier one, so each repetition is compared with its own starting state. In most tasks the event marks completion. In StopCube it signals an approaching target, and in ButtonUnmaskSwap Astra verifies a reported completion of the second button press (Appendix~ app:events ). Event-Triggered Coordination sec:coordination Astra is called once at initialization, and the monitor runs after every action chunk. A negative decision keeps the current instruction for another chunk. A completion event adds the subtask to the progress record and requests the next one. The StopCube timing event and the ButtonUnmaskSwap verification event send the execution history to Astra before the system advances. Figure~ fig:execution-compact shows instruction reuse across one completion event; Appendix~ app:visuals gives full walkthroughs. Inference scheduling. As in RoboMME's official two-system evaluation, the simulator pauses while Astra runs, so planning time adds to wall-clock duration but not to the step budget. In preliminary runs without pausing, the VLA used up the 1,300-step budget in most episodes before Astra returned. Experiments sec:experiments Setup. We evaluate on the official RoboMME test set (50 episodes per task) with a 1,300-step budget per episode and report simulator task success. Baseline numbers are the published RoboMME results~ dai2026robomme : ~ black2025pi05 with the current observation only; FrameSamp+Modul and SAM2Act+~ fang2025sam2act with perceptual memory; and MemER~ sridhar2026memer , GroundSG+QwenVL, and GroundSG+Gemini with a high-level planner. The last two use a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B~ qwen3vl and a prompted Gemini~2.5 Pro~ gemini25 . GroundSG+Oracle gives ground-truth subgoals to the low-level policy and serves as a reference for grounded execution. Astra uses medium reasoning effort; the VLA, monitor, and simulator share one NVIDIA L40S GPU. Task success. The system reaches 79.13 overall success (Table~ tab:results ): 94.00 on Permanence, 92.00 on Reference, 69.50 on Counting, and 61.00 on Imitation. Overall success is 34.62 points above FrameSamp+Modul, the best non-oracle baseline, and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle. The gap to the oracle is largest in Counting (14.36 points, versus 3.17 in Reference and 2.98 in Imitation), and it comes mostly from StopCube: the other three Counting tasks average 86.67 . Failure cases. Of the 167 unsuccessful episodes, 103 fail and 64 time out. StopCube and InsertPeg each succeed in only 9/50 episodes and together account for 82 of them. StopCube requires pressing a button on a specific passage of a moving cube; all 41 of its unsuccessful episodes are failures rather than timeouts. InsertPeg requires contact-rich insertion; 36 of its 41 unsuccessful episodes time out. We have not yet attributed these failures to planning, monitoring, or execution errors. Appendix~ app:results lists outcomes for all 16 tasks. Planner usage. The system averages 3.63 Astra calls per episode, counting both planning and visual-verification requests, and 80.84 seconds of wall-clock time. The recorded trajectories contain 24.62 action chunks on average, so calling Astra before every chunk would require about 24.62 calls along the same trajectories. Writing these averages as and , This figure assumes the recorded trajectories; a controller that replans at every chunk would follow different trajectories and could reach a different success rate. Call count is also only a proxy for cost, because request size grows with the supplied history and the monitor runs after every chunk. Limitations and Conclusion Limitations. We evaluate only the full system. Ablations that remove the history, replace Astra with a smaller planner, or replace the monitor with fixed-interval replanning are needed to separate the contributions of memory, planner capability, and monitoring. The GroundSG baselines differ from our system in planner, inputs, and replanning schedule, so they are not matched comparisons. We did not run an always-replan controller or measure token usage and monetary cost. We also did not measure the monitor's closed-loop error rate; a false completion corrupts the progress record used by later calls. History selection, output templates, and event rules are set per task, which limits transfer to new tasks. Finally, the simulator pauses during planning, so we have not tested scenes that change while Astra reasons. Conclusion. On RoboMME, the three-tier system reached 79.13 success while calling Astra 3.63 times per episode, compared with 24.62 action chunks. The ablations and cost measurements above would show which parts of the system account for this result. Implementation Details app:implementation Planner Inputs Image history is sent as sheets of up to 16 frames in a grid, each labeled with its frame index. Nine tasks receive the demonstration video: VideoUnmask, VideoUnmaskSwap, VideoRepick, VideoPlaceButton, VideoPlaceOrder, MoveCube, InsertPeg, PatternLock, and RouteStick. Four receive dense execution history: ButtonUnmask, ButtonUnmaskSwap, PickHighlight, and StopCube. In the first three, this history stops at the monitor-confirmed button press; only the current image is updated after that. StopCube receives every execution frame so that Astra can count the cube's passages. The remaining tasks (BinFill, PickXtimes, SwingXtimes) rely on the text progress record. Monitor Training The monitor is trained on 71,835 examples built from RoboMME demonstrations, labeled with the recorded subtask boundaries. For StopCube waiting subtasks, positive labels instead mark the interval just before the cube reaches the target. We fine-tune with LoRA (rank 16) on the language model, keeping the vision encoder frozen, for two epochs. Task-Specific Events app:events StopCube requires stopping a moving cube on a specified passage through the target. During a waiting subtask, the monitor fires about 16--32 environment steps before the cube reaches the target. Each trigger calls Astra, which counts the actual passages in the execution history and decides whether to keep waiting or press the button. In ButtonUnmaskSwap, when the monitor reports that the second button press is complete, Astra checks this against the execution history before the system advances; if Astra rejects it, the same instruction continues. Both prompts are in Appendix~ app:runtime . Deployment Astra runs with medium reasoning effort through Codex CLI. Calls are spaced at least 20 seconds apart. title: TwinBridge: Digital Twin-Driven Policy and Reward Transfer for Real-World Reinforcement Learning in Laboratory Robotics
summary: Online reinforcement learning offers an effective approach to precise laboratory manipulation, yet costly real-world demonstrations and limited access to dense process rewards hinder its practical application. We present TwinBridge, a digital twin-driven framework that supplies policy initialization and dense visual rewards for real-world online learning. We construct digital twins by combining 3D Gaussian splatting with physics simulation. Here, simulator states provide task events and geometric progress under physical prerequisites and ordering constraints, yielding rewards for policy pretraining with simulated demonstrations and reinforcement learning. We distill this supervision into a visual reward model. During real-world interaction, its predictions are combined with execution history to compute dense rewards for human-in-the-loop policy refinement. Across five real-world laboratory tasks, TwinBridge achieves a final mean autonomous success rate of 98% with at most 25 minutes of real-world interaction per task. Experiments show that dense rewards improve interaction efficiency over sparse rewards, and simulation-based policy initialization further accelerates learning.

title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

title: Robocasa-Mem: Benchmarking Environment and Process Memory in Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
summary: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.
full_text: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce , a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT- geometry into action generation. Together, and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies. 10 Project Page: \\ Code: \\ Data: Introduction sec:introduction Mobile manipulation requires robots to navigate between locations and interact with objects~ szot2021habitat,nasiriany2024robocasa . While tabletop manipulation often concentrates task-relevant information within a fixed workspace, mobile manipulation extends interactions across different work areas. As the robot moves and interacts with the environment, previously observed information may become inaccessible yet remain essential for subsequent decisions. For example, when cooking, a robot may need to remember whether it has already added salt to the pot after the salt has dissolved and is no longer visually distinguishable. Such situations motivate maintaining historical information about both the environment and task execution, beyond what is available in the current observation~ torne2026mem . Memory dependence is not equivalent to long-horizon manipulation. A task may involve multiple sequential steps without requiring historical information, provided that the current observation is sufficient for decision-making. Conversely, even a short task may require memory when critical information is no longer observable. From a partially observable decision-making perspective, historical information is needed when different interaction histories yield indistinguishable current observations but require different subsequent decisions~ kaelbling1998pomdp . We therefore evaluate memory based on the necessity of historical information for correct decision-making, rather than task length or execution complexity alone. Existing mobile-manipulation benchmarks, such as RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 , MS-HAB~ shukla2025maniskillhab , BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2024behavior1k , and the suite of works based on Habitat~ puig2023habitat3, szot2021habitat,habitat19iccv , primarily evaluate task execution, long-horizon control, generalization, and policy learning, without explicitly isolating decisions that require historical information. In parallel, robotic memory benchmarks such as RMBench~ chen2026rmbench , RoboMME~ dai2026robomme , RoboMemArena~ lei2026robomemarena , and RoboTwin-MeM~ yang2026eventvla study history-dependent manipulation, predominantly in tabletop or fixed-base settings. Mobile manipulation brings these memory demands into settings where robots move between work areas, lose visual access to previously observed entities, and must resume unfinished activities. Two requirements are particularly relevant: retaining object states established through earlier interactions but no longer visually distinguishable, and tracking progress and pending actions across interleaved activities in different regions. Although neither requirement is unique to mobile manipulation, their joint evaluation under changing viewpoints and cross-region execution remains limited. To systematically characterize these requirements, we organize memory into two complementary dimensions: Environment Memory and Process Memory. Environment Memory captures information about the physical environment that cannot be reliably recovered from the current observation, encompassing Spatial Memory, Attribute Memory, and Relational Memory. Process Memory tracks task execution states and information needed to determine subsequent actions, encompassing Single-Task Progress and Multi-Task Scheduling. This taxonomy explicitly accounts for visually unobservable object attribute changes and the scheduling of interleaved tasks, providing a systematic characterization of memory requirements in mobile manipulation. Based on this taxonomy, we introduce , a benchmark for memory in mobile manipulation. contains nine mobile-manipulation tasks covering the five memory categories above. Each task is designed to introduce observation-insufficient decision points, where the current observation alone cannot determine the appropriate action, requiring the robot to retrieve and utilize information from its interaction history. This design explicitly evaluates memory dependence rather than relying on task horizon as its proxy. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation, which derives later constraints from the policy's own earlier interactions rather than fixing a target in advance. This allows history-consistent behavior to be evaluated without prescribing a single execution trajectory. To provide a baseline, we develop a Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP) that combines structured memory for planning with geometry-augmented control. A high-level planner maintains Entity Memory and Process Memory to track environment states, execution progress, and pending actions, and generates executable subgoals. A low-level VLA controller executes these subgoals using current observations and multi-view geometric features extracted by VGGT- ~ wang2026vggtomega , which are incorporated through task-conditioned queries and action modulation. Across the nine tasks, HMAP improves average success from 16.2 to 24.2 over ~ black2025pi05 , with gains concentrated in hidden-attribute recall. Improvements on process-memory tasks remain inconsistent, highlighting challenges in progress tracking and interleaved execution. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=1.2em] Benchmark and dataset. We introduce , comprising nine mobile-manipulation tasks organized into five memory categories across environment-state and task-state memory, together with 1,800 successful demonstration trajectories for policy training. Evaluation protocol. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation, which derives subsequent semantic constraints from the robot's actual interactions to assess history-consistent behavior across multiple valid execution paths. We report both final task success and stage-level completion. Baseline and findings. We develop Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy (HMAP) that combines structured semantic memory for planning with 3D geometric feature for control. Our experiments reveal gains concentrated in hidden-attribute recall and identify persistent challenges in task-progress tracking and interleaved multi-task execution. Related Work sec:related-work Mobile-manipulation benchmarks. Existing benchmarks study diverse aspects of mobile manipulation, including task diversity, long-horizon execution, generalization, and scalable policy learning. RoboCasa and RoboCasa365 provide large-scale household environments, tasks, and demonstrations~ nasiriany2024robocasa,nasiriany2026robocasa365 ; Habitat 2.0 and MS-HAB focus on long-horizon household rearrangement and low-level mobile-manipulation control~ szot2021habitat,shukla2025maniskillhab ; and BEHAVIOR-1K covers a broad range of household activities and physical interactions~ li2024behavior1k . These benchmarks do not explicitly isolate memory dependence as an evaluation target. In contrast, focuses on decisions for which the current observation is insufficient and earlier information must be retained. Memory benchmarks for manipulation. Recent benchmarks explicitly evaluate memory in robotic manipulation. MIKASA-Robo and RMBench study memory-intensive manipulation tasks~ cherepanov2025mikasa,chen2026rmbench ; RoboMME evaluates temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory~ dai2026robomme ; RoboMemArena studies long-horizon manipulation with memory-related annotations~ lei2026robomemarena ; and RoboTwin-MeM considers non-Markovian tasks in which later actions depend on earlier visual observations~ yang2026eventvla . Most of these benchmarks focus on tabletop or fixed-base manipulation. instead targets mobile manipulation and emphasizes memory demands arising from changing environment states and interleaved task execution. It also evaluates history-dependent decisions without requiring a single predefined execution path. Memory-augmented embodied policies. Memory-augmented policies differ mainly in how historical information is selected and represented. MemER retrieves historical keyframes for high-level subtask generation, while EventVLA, KEMO, and UniMem retain task-relevant or event-triggered observations for later prediction and control~ sridhar2025memer,yang2026eventvla,zeng2026kemo,osterberg2026unimem . Other methods combine memory across temporal or semantic scales: MemoryVLA uses working and perceptual-cognitive memory, MEM combines short-term video memory with long-term textual memory, and Mimir separates world memory from task memory~ shi2025memoryvla,torne2026mem,xu2026mimir . Our method similarly uses memory at high levels and combines persistent structured memory for high-level task decisions with current 3D visual features for low-level control. For example, after sugar dissolves in water, the current image does not reveal whether sugar was previously added to a cup. The policy must therefore retain information from earlier interactions rather than relying only on the current observation. This distinguishes memory dependence from task horizon: a task may contain many steps without requiring memory if each decision can still be made from the current observation. title: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
summary: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.
