Introduction sec:intro Soccer stands apart from sports such as table tennis~ su2025hitter,ren2026smash and tennis~ zhang2026learningathletichumanoidtennis as a uniquely demanding benchmark for humanoid robots: rather than isolating upper-body dexterity, it demands the inseparable coupling of agile whole-body locomotion and non-prehensile ball manipulation across a rich, continuous behavioral spectrum. Humans master this spectrum with remarkable fluency: sprinting, trapping, dribbling, and kicking compose seamlessly into a continuous, expressive behavioral repertoire. This fluency emerges from decades of motor learning that endows human motion with natural coordination, dynamic stability, and graceful skill transitions. Replicating such fluency on a humanoid robot is far from trivial: the robot must not only master a diverse set of highly dynamic skills, but also execute smooth, natural transitions across the full behavioral spectrum. Humanoid soccer thus emerges as a compelling platform for studying unified whole-body control, simultaneously demanding agile locomotion, non-prehensile object manipulation, impact-rich contact dynamics, and human-like motion quality within a single, coherent control problem. Despite recent progress in reinforcement learning for humanoid locomotion~ radosavovic2024humanoid,radosavovic2024learning,radosavovic2024real and motor skill acquisition~ peng2021amp,peng2022ase,liao2025beyondmimic,ji2024exbody2,li2026omnitrack,yang2025omniretarget,wang2026omnixtreme,haarnoja2024learning , existing approaches to humanoid soccer remain fundamentally limited along two orthogonal axes. On one axis, existing methods lack a unified skill repertoire: most prior works address only a narrow subset of soccer behaviors~ kong2026learning,wang2026learning,wang2026dribble , such as directed kicking, dribbling, or locomotion-only control, and even multi-skill systems rely on decoupled, independently trained controllers that cannot naturally bridge the dynamics between different actions~ kim2025physicsfc . Multi-skill soccer built on human motion priors has so far been demonstrated only for simulated characters~ liu2022motor,kim2025physicsfc . The result is a fragmented behavioral space where inter-skill transitions are inherently discontinuous and unnatural, as evidenced by the jarring switches between running and trapping, or dribbling and kicking. On the other axis, many existing methods rely solely on task-reward-driven reinforcement learning without any motion prior~ haarnoja2024learning , leaving motion naturalness entirely unaddressed. Without structural regularization grounded in human motion, such policies produce erratic, mechanically unnatural behaviors that are both visually implausible and brittle under the contact-rich dynamics of real soccer interaction. Together, these two axes define a clear gap in the literature: the combination of human-like coordination and a complete, unified soccer skill set has never been simultaneously achieved in a single humanoid soccer system. To close this gap, we propose , a hierarchical learning framework that addresses both limitations through a unified mechanism: a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. Building on recent advances in physics-based motion imitation~ luo2024universal , we first distill a motion tracking policy into a compact latent action space that encodes a rich, dynamically plausible manifold of human-like whole-body motion. A unified skill-conditioned policy then operates within this latent space via residual control, learning to perform dribbling, trapping, kicking, and moving under a shared control formulation. By grounding all skills within the same motion prior, inherently produces natural, human-like motion across the full behavioral spectrum, and produces fluid, natural inter-skill transitions during commanded skill switching. To further support reliable real-world deployment, we incorporate robustness-oriented simulation design including ball dynamics modeling, domain randomization, and observation perturbation, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. We evaluate in both simulation and real-world settings, demonstrating that a single unified policy can execute the full spectrum of soccer skills with agility and naturalness under real-world conditions. The main contributions of this work are as follows: [leftmargin=*,noitemsep,nolistsep,topsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] We present , to our knowledge the first real-world humanoid soccer system that jointly achieves a complete skill repertoire and human-like motion quality, learning moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking within a single unified policy. We propose a hierarchical latent motion prior framework with transition state initialization (TSI), grounding unified soccer skill learning within a structured motion manifold and enabling agile, human-like behaviors, fluid inter-skill transitions, and robust cross-skill composition without explicit state machines or separate controllers. We conduct extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1, demonstrating strong task performance across all four skills, structured latent skill-space organization, and reliable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with minimal performance degradation. Videos are available at . Related Work sec:related_work Humanoid control and athletic skills. Reinforcement learning has driven rapid progress in humanoid robot control, enabling robust locomotion~ radosavovic2024real,radosavovic2024humanoid,radosavovic2024learning and whole-body motion tracking~ liao2025beyondmimic,ji2024exbody2,chen2025gmt,zhang2025track,wang2026omnixtreme,li2026omnitrack from large-scale human motion capture data~ mahmood2019amass . Beyond locomotion and motion tracking, RL has enabled humanoid robots to master a growing range of athletic skills, including tennis~ zhang2026learningathletichumanoidtennis , table tennis~ su2025hitter,ren2026smash , and parkour~ wu2026perceptive,yang2025omniretarget . Among these, humanoid soccer stands out as uniquely demanding: it requires the tight coupling of agile locomotion and non-prehensile ball manipulation through the feet, sustained across a continuous and dynamic behavioral spectrum. Early learning-based soccer systems demonstrated agile ball interaction on simulated avatars~ liu2022motor and small real bipedal robots~ haarnoja2024learning , while more recent work has explored soccer motion generation from human demonstrations~ vahl2025soccerdiffusion, yang2025smgdiff . On real humanoid robots, Dribble Master~ wang2026dribble learns agile dribbling through a two-stage curriculum with virtual-camera perception, and other works study perception-driven kicking and reactive soccer skills~ kong2026learning,wang2026learning . Most closely related to our work, PhysicsFC~ kim2025physicsfc learns dribbling, trapping, moving, and kicking with smooth transitions, but relies on skill-specific policies with an explicit finite-state machine and remains confined to simulation. In contrast, our work learns a single unified policy across the full soccer skill repertoire and deploys it on a real humanoid robot. Latent motion priors for humanoid control. A prominent approach to regularizing humanoid reinforcement learning uses adversarial motion priors. AMP~ peng2021amp learns a discriminator from unstructured motion clips to provide a style reward that guides task policies toward natural behaviors, and ASE~ peng2022ase extends this by learning reusable adversarial skill embeddings for downstream task policies. While effective, adversarial approaches require careful balancing between task reward and motion realism, and can struggle to discover precise contact-rich strategies such as ball trapping. An alternative line of work constructs structured latent action spaces by distilling motion tracking controllers into compact motor representations. PULSE~ luo2024universal distills a universal humanoid motion tracker into a VAE-style latent action space with a learned state-conditioned prior, enabling downstream policies to generate coherent human-like motions without adversarial rewards. Inspired by this framework, recent work has extended latent motion priors to athletic humanoid skills, demonstrating their effectiveness for contact-rich tasks such as tennis~ zhang2026learningathletichumanoidtennis . We adapt the latent motion prior framework to unified humanoid soccer, training a single residual latent policy conditioned on skill commands across moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking, which extends beyond single-skill athletic tasks to a complete soccer skill repertoire deployed on a real robot. Method sec:method We present , a staged framework for learning a unified whole-body policy for humanoid soccer skills. The key idea is to separate low-level motor competence from high-level soccer task optimization. As shown in~ , our pipeline has three stages: Stage~I trains a motion tracking teacher from curated soccer demonstrations; Stage~II distills this teacher into a compact latent motion prior; and Stage~III trains a skill-conditioned soccer policy within this frozen latent action space. The final policy receives a skill command and task observation, predicts a latent residual, and decodes it into joint position targets through the pretrained motion decoder. We source human soccer demonstrations from Soccer-X~ yang2025smgdiff and retarget them to the humanoid robot using GMR~ joao2025gmr . title: Which Physical Tactile Cues Matter for Contact-Rich Imitation Learning? A Controlled Real-Robot Study

summary: Vision-based tactile sensors capture multiple aspects of physical interaction within a single image stream, including contact appearance, geometry, indentation depth, and tangential deformation. However, existing visuo-tactile policies often directly process tactile observations as images, making it difficult to determine which physical cues contribute to policy learning. This paper presents a controlled real-robot study that compares physically interpretable tactile signals using the LeRobot platform, enhanced with our visuo-tactile perception system. From the same tactile stream, we derive tactile RGB images, normal/depth maps, and marker-flow fields, representing contact appearance, geometry, and tangential deformation, respectively. Using identical task demonstrations and the same policy backbone, we evaluate the individual and combined contributions of these tactile cues. We further compare tactile encoders and visuo-tactile fusion strategies. Evaluation across 720 real-robot trials yields four key findings: (1) tactile perception substantially improves the overall success rate from 57.8% to 78.9%, although its contribution varies across task stages; (2) marker flow is the most effective individual cue, achieving a success rate of 74.4% and playing a particularly important role in regulating established contact; (3) cue-factorized encoding consistently improves performance, highlighting that different physical cues require tailored processing techniques; and (4) although the effectiveness of tactile fusion is task-dependent, cross-attention offers a lightweight solution with performance comparable to that of pretrained tactile encoders.

Introduction Visuomotor imitation learning has achieved strong performance across a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks~ chi2025diffusion . However, successful manipulation often depends on local physical interaction states that are only partially observable by external cameras. Contact regions may be occluded by the robot or the manipulated object, while subtle indentation, tangential deformation, slip, and contact stability may remain visually ambiguous. Tactile feedback helps bridge this gap by directly observing local interactions and has therefore become increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation~ calandra2018more,dong2021tactile,yu2024mimictouch,xue2025reactive . In this paper, we focus on vision-based tactile sensors, which image the deformation of a compliant elastomer to provide dense observations of the contact interface~ yuan2017gelsight,lambeta2020digit,taylor2022gelslim . Unlike conventional visual images, tactile images arise from physical interaction and encode several distinct forms of contact information. RGB images capture tactile appearance, including contact patterns and color variations induced by elastomer deformation; surface-normal and depth maps describe contact geometry; and marker-displacement fields capture tangential deformation. We refer to these explicit input forms as , distinguishing them from the latent representations learned by tactile encoders. Despite their different physical meanings, tactile observations are commonly processed as raw RGB images using generic image encoders, leaving unclear which underlying signals support policy learning. Prior work has investigated tactile-specific encoders, visuo-tactile fusion, and broader policy-learning benchmarks~ higuera2024sparsh, gupta2025sensorinvariant,heng2025vitacformerlearningcrossmodalrepresentation,luu2025manifeel . These studies primarily examine how complete tactile observations are encoded, integrated, or evaluated, rather than isolating the contributions of their constituent physical signals. In contrast, we systematically evaluate the individual and joint roles of tactile appearance, contact geometry, and tangential deformation derived from the same tactile observations under matched learning conditions. Specifically, we ask which signals are most informative for policy learning and whether their combinations provide complementary benefits. Beyond informing representation choice, this analysis offers practical guidance for tactile-sensor design by identifying which tactile cues should be prioritized under different contact regimes and when multiple cues should be jointly retained. To address these questions, we derive RGB, surface-normal/depth, marker-flow, and combined signal representations from the same real-world tactile stream. We compare these representations using identical demonstrations, visual observations, and policy backbones. We then fix the tactile input to the combined representation and compare generic image encoders with tactile-pretrained encoders, as well as concatenation-based and cross-attention-based fusion. This staged experimental design compares tactile input representations and evaluates encoder and fusion choices under fixed full-tactile input. Our experiments yield these main findings. First, tactile perception substantially improves overall policy performance, although the utility of individual tactile cues varies across interaction stages. Second, marker flow is the strongest individual cue overall, with qualitative failure analysis suggesting its potential role in regulating established contact, whereas normal/depth cues appear more useful for contact establishment. Although full tactile provides only a modest improvement over marker flow in final success rate, combining these cues promotes smoother and more continuous transitions across interaction stages. Third, while the effectiveness of visuo-tactile fusion remains task-dependent, cue-factorized encoding, and cross-attention consistently improve performance, and provide a lightweight alternative with performance comparable to tactile-pretrained encoding. In summary, this work makes three contributions: 0pt 0pt 0pt We introduce an open, LeRobot-compatible visuo-tactile testbed with a standardized Diffusion Policy pipeline for reproducible evaluation of tactile signal representations. We conduct a comparative study of the individual and joint roles of tactile appearance, contact geometry, and tangential deformation, showing that marker flow is the strongest individual cue overall and that the utility of different tactile cues varies across interaction stages. We systematically compare generic and tactile-pretrained encoders and visuo-tactile fusion strategies with fixed tactile inputs, showing that cross-attention offers a simple, lightweight option that balances performance and complexity. Related Work Vision-based Tactile Sensors Vision-based tactile sensors have become an important sensing modality for robotic manipulation. Representative sensors, including GelSight~ yuan2017gelsight , GelSlim~ taylor2022gelslim , and DIGIT~ lambeta2020digit , provide dense, localized contact information by imaging the deformation of a compliant surface. Existing sensors adopt different sensing recipes that expose distinct physical cues: photometric designs use controlled illumination and reflective elastomers to reconstruct contact geometry through photometric stereo~ johnson2009retrographic , whereas marker-based sensors such as FingerVision track dot motion to capture force- and slip-related cues~ yamaguchi2019tactile , and TacForce maps marker deformation to dense force distributions~ duong2024tacforce . Marker-free designs emphasize tactile RGB appearance, while hybrid designs combine photometric geometry and marker motion. However, which combination of appearance, geometry, and deformation cues best supports policy learning remains unclear. Our sensor combines calibrated illumination with a marker-embedded elastomer, allowing these cues to be derived from the same tactile stream and compared under matched conditions. Visuo-Tactile Learning for Contact-Rich Manipulation Existing visuo-tactile manipulation methods differ in when and how tactile information is incorporated into the policy and control loop. Early work demonstrated that tactile sensing improves grasping, regrasping, and insertion by providing contact information unavailable from vision alone~ calandra2018more,dong2021tactile . More recent imitation-learning systems have leveraged tactile feedback for fine-grained assembly, reactive policy learning, and contact-aware manipulation. MimicTouch~ yu2024mimictouch uses multimodal human demonstrations with tactile feedback for contact-rich tasks, while Reactive Diffusion Policy~ xue2025reactive introduces a slow--fast visuo-tactile architecture for rapid tactile responses. Although these studies demonstrate different ways of exploiting tactile feedback, they typically rely on a fixed tactile representation tailored to a particular sensor, task, or policy architecture. Building on their evidence that touch benefits contact-rich manipulation, we investigate which tactile cues are most useful for imitation learning. Tactile Representation Learning and Visuo-Tactile Fusion Recent work has moved beyond handcrafted tactile features toward tactile-specific representation learning. Sparsh~ higuera2024sparsh learns general-purpose tactile representations through self-supervised pretraining on vision-based tactile data, while SITR~ gupta2025sensorinvariant investigates sensor-invariant representations across sensors and tasks. In parallel, visuo-tactile fusion models study how local tactile cues should interact with visual scene information. ViTacFormer~ heng2025vitacformerlearningcrossmodalrepresentation uses cross-modal attention to learn coupled visual and tactile representations, ManiFeel~ luu2025manifeel benchmarks tactile modalities, encoders, and policy architectures across simulated and real-world tasks, and CONTACT~ saka2026contact compares tactile RGB with an aggregated normal--shear force-field representation for robotic disassembly. Complementing these studies, we compare tactile RGB, normal/depth geometry, marker-flow, and their combination under identical learning conditions; and subsequently, examine the performance of different design choices for visuo-tactile fusion. Method System Overview The overall framework is shown in Fig.~ fig:system_overview , which consists of a LeRobot platform augmented with visuo-tactile sensing for data collection, and a Diffusion Policy pipeline. The platform synchronously records global-camera images, wrist-camera images, robot proprioception, actions, and tactile observations. The same tactile stream is then converted into tactile RGB, normal/depth, and marker-flow representations. Within the shared policy framework, these representations are processed by modality-specific frontends and fused with visual and proprioceptive features for action prediction. This unified design enables controlled comparisons of tactile cue representations, tactile-RGB encoders, and visuo-tactile fusion strategies under matched demonstrations and policy settings,while modality-specific frontends differ across some tactile input configurations. Hardware Platform and Data Collection As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:system_overview , we build a LeRobot-compatible visuo-tactile parallel-jaw gripper for collecting contact-rich demonstrations. One fingertip is equipped with a vision-based tactile sensor consisting of a marker-embedded elastomer, an internal camera, and calibrated illumination, while the opposite jaw provides passive mechanical support. The tactile sensor is integrated into the gripper structure to capture contact-induced deformation during manipulation. During demonstration collection, the system synchronizes global-camera images, wrist-camera images, robot proprioception, actions, and tactile observations from the tactile-equipped fingertip within the LeRobot framework. These multimodal observations are stored in a unified LeRobot dataset format. title: When to Ask for Help: Uncertainty-Triggered Aerial Refinement for Off-Road Navigation
summary: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Introduction Ground vehicles operating alone in outdoor, unstructured environments are limited by their sensing perspective, mobility, and onboard perception. Ground-level sensors have limited range, suffer from occlusion, and can provide incomplete or ambiguous information about terrain, obstacles, and vehicle state. An unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) may therefore fail to complete an otherwise achievable mission because it cannot obtain the information needed to navigate safely and reliably. Heterogeneous robot teams address this by combining complementary sensing and mobility. An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) can observe the environment and the ground vehicle from viewpoints unavailable to the UGV and provide information that improves the ground robot's navigation state. However, UAV assistance is limited by flight endurance and cannot be used continuously throughout long missions. The key problem is therefore deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should provide. This paper presents a heterogeneous air--ground teaming approach for recovering degraded UGV navigation caused by incomplete or uncertain information in off-road environments. The UGV maintains separate navigation map layers together with their associated uncertainty. When navigation degrades, we evaluate the current MPPI rollout population~ williams2016aggressive against counterfactual versions of these map layers and score how the resulting map changes affect predicted ground motion. We then select the corresponding UAV sensing action for the map layer with the largest useful improvement. The UAV collects the requested aerial information, such as an elevation map or semantic map, and communicates it to the UGV. The UGV fuses the information into its navigation maps, updates the planner representation, and replans. Existing air-ground systems use heterogeneous sensing for cooperative localization, mapping, exploration, and navigation. Many approaches assign the UAV a fixed support role, invoke aerial sensing according to predefined task logic, or trigger additional sensing from uncertainty in a perception output garzon2013aerialground . These sensing criteria do not directly determine whether the uncertainty affects the UGV's current navigation decision. Uncertainty can be large in regions that have no effect on the current route, while localized uncertainty can prevent the UGV from identifying or executing a safe path. We therefore evaluate uncertainty through its effect on ground navigation and request UAV assistance only when resolving uncertainty is predicted to improve the UGV's ability to make progress. Our main contribution, illustrated in Figure~ fig:hero-picture , is a planner-conditioned air--ground assistance method that determines when the UAV should sense by evaluating resolved map hypotheses against current UGV rollouts and selecting an aerial sensing action based on the change in navigation score. Across 180 simulation trials, our method achieves 98.9 goal attainment with 87.7 less mean UAV flight time than continuous greedy mapping. Across three routes, each estimated UAV flight second saves of UGV navigation time. Autonomous navigation in unstructured outdoor environments requires a ground robot to reason about obstacles, terrain, vehicle state, and long-range route structure from incomplete onboard observations. Early off-road autonomy systems identified limited sensing lookahead and terrain interpretation as fundamental constraints on ground navigation howard2007traversability,bajracharya2009lagr . Recent work has improved long-range planning through learned cost maps trailblazer2025 , terrain--vehicle interaction models anynav2025 , and increasingly capable local planners evaluated under physical field conditions majhor2025muons . These approaches improve the information available to the ground-navigation stack, but the sensing geometry and mobility of the UGV continue to limit what can be observed from the ground. We consider failures that arise when these information limitations prevent an otherwise capable navigation stack from identifying or executing useful motion. Air--Ground Teaming. Air--ground teams use the complementary sensing and mobility of aerial and ground platforms to extend the capabilities of either platform operating independently. Early systems used UAVs as forward scouts to detect hazards beyond the sensing horizon of an off-road UGV stentz2002flyingeye,delmerico2017activeexploration,zhang2022fastactive , while subsequent work has considered heterogeneous teams for perception, exploration, localization, mapping, and navigation zhou2026survey . Recent approaches increasingly adapt aerial sensing to the state of the task. UAV imagery has been used to construct obstacle maps and guide UGV motion in large outdoor environments kim2013collaborative,garzon2013aerialground , while cooperative mapping systems fuse aerial and ground observations to improve environmental coverage kim2019cooperativemapping . Related approaches use inter-platform measurements to improve localization, including active motion strategies for positioning geometry sivaneri2017uavugv,sivaneri2018flighttest . Recent work couples aerial perception more directly to UGV navigation. Fortin et al.\ estimate off-road terrain properties from aerial imagery to construct traversability information for subsequent UGV path planning fortin2025uavterrain . Counterfactual reasoning has also been applied to navigation: CREStE rewards navigation aligned with human preferences using counterfactual trajectory annotations zhang2025creste , and CoINS reasons about hypothetical object removal to decide when physical intervention is needed to create a traversable path zhou2026coins . Our approach instead evaluates hypothetical resolutions of map uncertainty by their effect on the ground planner, an optimistic form of value of information~ howard1966information applied to deciding when a robot should ask for help~ tellex2014asking , with a UAV rather than a human as the helper. The UGV scores its current planner rollouts under counterfactual resolutions of each uncertain map layer and requests aerial sensing only when a resolution yields sufficient improvement in predicted ground motion. title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are multimodal models that enable robots to translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into executable actions, such as moving an arm or opening a gripper. They typically build on pretrained vision-language models that are trained on robot demonstrations, connecting visual and semantic knowledge with the physical skills needed to perform tasks~ zitkovich2023rt . VLAs aim to support general-purpose robots that can follow diverse instructions and generalize to unfamiliar objects and environments~ openvla,pi05 . Internally, VLAs typically run a VLM with millions or billions of parameters to generate the robot's control steps. This limits the reaction time of a robot by the inference latency of the VLA. At each policy inference step, a typical VLA receives a natural-language instruction, represented as text, and image observations from one or more cameras. In a common architecture, a vision encoder converts camera images into visual embeddings, which are projected into the language model’s embedding space and processed jointly with the instruction tokens by a transformer backbone. The resulting representations condition the prediction of a robot action or a short sequence of actions with the action generations performed using an action-head. VLAs need to be real-time, providing a robot with a sufficient number of actions such that the robot does not stall. Robots typically operate with strictly bounded latencies to maintain a continuous, closed-loop feedback cycle. In addition, if a VLA is too slow, it acts on stale visual data, i.e., by the time the model computes and outputs a command, the physical world has already changed leading to dropped objects, collisions, or unstable movement. This is challenging, especially when the VLA is running on the limited on-robot hardware. One approach to reduce the computational time of VLAs is to use optimization methods such as, token pruning, quantization, compilation, or CUDA graphs. However, our study of 25 published paper (Appendix app:audit ) reveals that most of these approaches do not consider the intricacies of the different VLA architectures and the hardware they run on. VLAs today vary in architecture, backbone size, visual token count and action path. These choices decide which stage dominates latency and therefore which optimization can help. The backbone size sets how many weight bytes every pass must read, so a large model could spend most of its time reading the model weights, whereas a smaller model could spend its time in the denoising loop of action head. In addition, previous work on VLA optimizations does not consider the inherent bottlenecks of the underlying hardware platform projecting generality of the results while only evaluating the work on a limited set of hardware. For example, many previous works evaluate the optimizations on GPUs such as NVIDIA RTX 4090s, a GPU that has a heavy weight and high power draw---it is neither designed for running on a robot platform nor is available on most clouds, hence, not supporting a cloud-robotic deployment. In this work, we provide a comprehensive study of VLA optimization performance. We start by analyzing seven families of inference optimization methods, namely; CUDA graphs, compilation, fused attention, batching, reducing the denoising steps, token pruning and quantization. We evaluate these optimizations on seven VLAs, namely; OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, LLaVA-VLA, CogACT, , GR00T, and SmolVLA, with four kinds of action head (token decoding, parallel decoding, diffusion, flow matching). These combinations are then tested on four different GPU families; a datacenter grade H100, a cloud A10G, a consumer RTX 4090, and an embedded Jetson Thor. Our evaluations focus on the latency gains of these optimizations, showing that the optimization results are non-uniform. Gains differ between GPUs in magnitude, in sign and in rank. For example, compiling GR00T with CUDA graphs makes it faster on the H100 and slower on the Thor, and storing CogACT's weights in 8 bits makes it faster on the A10G and slower on the H100. In addition, we find that the choice of baseline to compare an optimization method to can be misleading, e.g., FastV~ fastv and several other token pruning methods (Appendix app:audit ) select the visual tokens to prune by their attention weights, so it is typically evaluated and compared to running with unfused attention. However, VLAs in production are often deployed with fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention-2~ flashattention2 , which never write attention weights to memory. Measured against unfused attention, FastV at pruning saves of OpenVLA-OFT's inference time on an H100. Measured against FlashAttention-2, the same run saves , because the selector reads attention weights and forces the slower kernel (Table~ tab:selector ). Our analysis also shows that each stage of inference is limited by either the GPU compute power, its memory bandwidth, or the CPU that launches the GPU kernels. This means that the same stage can be subject to a different bottleneck on different GPUs. Therefore, a proposed optimization method's benefit may not extend beyond the platform it is tested on. In addition, optimization methods can be combined, or stacked. Hence, running multiple optimizations in sequence means that later VLA optimizations act on the inference stages that are left by previous optimizations. Hence, the total gains from a later method depends on the methods applied before it. Based on the above observations, we formalize VLA-Triage, a systematic approach for evaluating the expected gains of multiple VLA optimization methods on a given hardware. To summarize, our paper has three connected contributions: Characterisation: paired measurements of inference-stage costs and optimization benefits across seven VLAs and four GPU-host platforms, including cases where a method helps on one platform and hurts on another. Interactions: We show how graphs, compilation and pruning change the gains for later applied methods, and how reusing standalone gains can change latency-budget decisions. Guidelines: A measurement-based workflow for choosing an execution mode, checking feasibility under stated assumptions, and validating method combinations to be used in deployment. After that, the language backbone processes these tokens together with the task instructions; this stage is called prefill. Finally, an action-generation stage produces the robot's commands. A chunk is a sequence of actions produced by one inference, so the robot can execute several control steps before requesting another prediction. One of the main differences between VLA models is in how they generate actions. This can be categorized in three main model categories: Autoregressive decoding models, e.g., OpenVLA~ openvla and LLaVA-VLA~ llavavla : Represent actions as a sequence of tokens, generated one per forward pass. Prefill-heavy models, e.g., OpenVLA-OFT~ openvlaoft and CogACT~ cogact : Run the language backbone once during prefill. title: Dexterous Robotic Hands in the Foundation-Model Era: A Full-Stack Survey of Hardware, Data, Cross-Embodiment Transfer, Learning, and Evaluation
comment: 45 pages, 8 figures, 21 tables. Structured narrative review of hardware, data, cross-embodiment transfer, foundation models, tactile sensing, and evaluation for dexterous robotic hands
summary: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.

Introduction sec:intro The human hand is the interface through which most of the built world is operated: tools, containers, fasteners, cables, keyboards and laboratory glassware are all designed around five fingers, opposable thumbs and a sense of touch. Building robot hands that can use this world without redesigning it has been a goal of robotics for decades~ okamura,piazza,controzzi,billard . For most of that time, progress was limited on three fronts at once. Anthropomorphic hands were expensive, fragile and hard to maintain (the Shadow Dexterous Hand~ shadowhand costs more than US\ 6.5k~ unitreedex5s , a six-DoF linkage hand for under US\ 10^3 10^5 n + 1 n 3k) ships with a simulation model and teleoperation pipeline~ midas . The main limitations are heat, limited per-finger force and the cost of 16--20 small motors. Linkage. Micro linear actuators drive coupled linkages, typically giving 6 active of 11--12 total DoF. Linkage hands are stiff, strong, durable and cheap, and dominate early humanoid deployments; their coupling limits in-hand dexterity and abduction. A six-DoF hand of this type is sold for about US\ 400 while reaching the maximum Kapandji score and all 33 grasp types~ hw_dexlink , and SyLink uses motion capture to find human joint correlations and decouples flexion from abduction with a spherical four-bar mechanism, driving 19 joints with 11 actuators at 520\,g~ hw_sylink . Tendon drive. Motors in the forearm pull tendons (often sheathed) that act on the fingers, as in the Shadow Hand~ shadowhand . This keeps the hand light and compliant and makes high DoF counts feasible, at the price of friction, creep, slack and a non-linear joint--motor map that needs tensioning and calibration. Tesla's Optimus V3 hand, according to patent analyses, moves 22 hand DoF onto 25 forearm actuators per arm and introduces a wrist routing that limits tendon-length change under combined yaw and pitch~ teslav3 . Open-source tendon hands focus on maintainability: ORCA uses joints that dislocate before they break, self-calibrating tendon routing and a ratchet tensioner, and ran 10 , 000 consecutive cycles without failure~ orcahand ; RUKA uses an underactuated tendon design and RUKA-v2 adds a parallel wrist~ ruka,rukav2 ; MM-Hand moves the motors to a remote housing with quick-release tendon connectors and analyzes sheath friction~ mmhand ; CRAFT combines soft joints with rigid links for under US\ 2k and a four-hour assembly, and outperformed the Allegro Hand at roughly one eighth of its cost~ leaphand . Since 2025, designs ship with what a learning pipeline needs: simulation models (Aero Hand Open is released ``simulation-ready'' at US\ 1.5k--6.1k~ orcacommercial . Hands are also being co-designed with data collection and with policies: RAPID Hand co-optimizes hand, perception and teleoperation interface~ rapidhand , and House of Dextra pretrains a morphology-conditioned policy over many generated hand shapes to evaluate candidate designs~ houseofdextra . Durability, cost and supply chain sec:hw-durability Durability is the first deployment bottleneck. Integrators report that some popular hands fail after about 50 grasps of a 5\,kg object; a warehouse robot performs 8 , 000--10 , 000 grasps per day while leading products are rated for 300k--500k cycles, which suggests a potential mismatch with continuous duty, but cannot by itself establish replacement intervals without matched loads and failure definitions~ yicaireliability . Figure reported that the forearm was the most common failure point in its BMW pilot~ figure03 . Vendor claims of 300k cycles~ wujihand,dexrobot sit near today's passing line; industrial deployment will require million-cycle lifetimes, load-specified test conditions and modular quick-swap designs. Cost. A complete low-cost bimanual research platform illustrates where money goes: about US\ 7k for the teleoperation system and US\ 16k--100k or more~ shadowhand,allegro,wujihand , while the 22-DoF Dex5-S is reported at about US\ 600 platform~ dep_airexo2 . Bidex extends ALOHA-style leader--follower setups to two dexterous hands on arms (more than 50 DoF in total) with mocap gloves and teacher arms, collecting better data faster than headset-based systems~ dep_bidex ; modular mobile teleoperation interfaces~ dep_telemoma and whole-body humanoid systems with learned, tuning-free hand retargeting~ dep_humdex broaden coverage. Kinesthetic hand-over-hand teaching is another route: KineDex transfers the operator's finger motion directly to the hand with tactile signals, collects data more than twice as fast as teleoperation on two tasks and reaches 74.4 success on contact-rich tasks with force-controlled deployment~ dep_kinedex . Large teleoperated corpora. Teleoperation also underpins large multi-embodiment datasets such as RoboMIND~ robomind and AgiBot World (more than one million trajectories and 2 , 976 hours from 100 robots, some with six-DoF hands)~ agibotworld , and initial versions of industrial VLAs~ figurehelix02 . The common bottleneck is that throughput equals the number of robots times operating hours, collection is confined to labs or data factories, and operators do not touch the objects, so demonstrations lack human contact strategies. Retargeting, haptics and shared autonomy sec:data-retarget Retargeting algorithms. Retargeting maps operator hand motion to robot joints in real time and is a hidden source of demonstration quality. A systematic ablation of the factors in retargeting objectives, together with a proposed combined objective, concludes that full reproduction of human motion is impossible because of mechanical differences~ dep_retargetobj . Recent algorithms add structure: Kilohertz-Safe formulates retargeting as a convex quadratic program in joint-velocity space with linearized joint-limit and collision constraints and control barrier functions, achieving 9.05\,ms average latency with more than 95 of frames meeting safety criteria on a 20-DoF hand~ dep_kilohertz ; ResPilot learns a residual Gaussian-process correction on top of keypoint optimization from 24 calibration poses (about 4.5 minutes per operator), enlarging the reachable fingertip workspace enough to enable finger gaiting~ dep_respilot ; EFOLD learns retargeting with deep RL, with command-following delay below 0.11\,s~ dep_efold ; DexTwist recognizes tripod pinches and estimates the intended screw axis for twisting tasks~ dep_dextwist ; and offline pipelines add temporal consistency and contact maps for data generation~ dep_dexflow . Hardware-agnostic frameworks aim at ``any arm, any hand, any input device''~ dep_openteledex,anyteleop . Haptic feedback. Feedback improves demonstrations, but the evidence base is small. Early gripper studies found that haptic feedback raised door-opening collection throughput by 6 and the success of resulting policies by about 11 ~ dep_cuanhaptic . On a dexterous hand, ViHaTeleop's US\ N 200 gloves whose geometry and sensors match its robot hand into robot data, and reports about ten million episodes from more than 2 , 000 contributors~ sundayact1,sunday36kr ; Generalist collects with wearable pincer-style ``data hands'', with press reports of growth from about 270k to more than 500k hours~ gen15,generalistprofile ; Liber-0 uses a 131\,g, 0.3\,mm skin-colored glove with egocentric and two wrist cameras~ liber0 ; and Genesis AI pairs a sensorized glove with a hand that mirrors it~ genesisai . Collection-hardware product families are also appearing on the market~ fastumi . Egocentric human video sec:data-ego Egocentric data record humans performing everyday tasks with head-mounted cameras, glasses or headsets; actions are recovered from estimated 3D hand poses. General-purpose corpora such as Ego4D~ ego4d , Ego-Exo4D~ egoexo4d and HOT3D~ hot3d provide limited hand annotation. EgoDex (829\,h, 194 tasks) records native 3D hand and finger tracking from Apple Vision Pro and is the most hand-relevant public dataset~ egodex . title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $ε$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $ετ$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $ε$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?

summary: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

Introduction sec:intro Code-as-policy agents translate language instructions into executable robot programs liang2023cap . Their failures often follow clear patterns: a program may skip the grasp, release an object after lifting, or place it away from the target. A common response is iterative self-reflection. The model reads its failed program and execution trace, writes a critique, and tries again shinn2023reflexion,madaan2023selfrefine,chen2024selfdebug . Retry success can reflect additional sampling, concise task instructions, feedback about the current failure, or editing the previous program. We ask whether feedback after failure improves recovery over guidance available from the first attempt. We study this question with frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B models in a reset-and-retry setting. Each retry starts from the original scene. Our main conditions generate a fresh program with the failed program omitted from the prompt. We use template-based feedback to study which information improves retry success. A fixed lookup selects instructions using the failure label and API variant, such as ``MUST grasp the object before lifting.'' We call this condition Compiled. The lookup lets us replace matched feedback with another episode's feedback, hold the guidance fixed, or remove it while keeping the retry loop unchanged (Figure~ fig:main ). Separate editing conditions expose the previous program and request a revision. All conditions restart the original scene. We do not test recovery from the physical state left by failure. Compiled recovers 85.3 of the 252 initial failures within five retries, compared with 68.3 for resampling with the same retry cap. The gain persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and one fixed template per task produce similar point estimates. We detect no benefit from matching the coarse failure label to the current episode. The confidence intervals still allow differences between conditions. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to Compiled's, with fewer tokens per solved episode. That comparison changes initial guidance and the generation instruction together. Their individual contributions remain unresolved. We compare feedback content and program-generation strategies under matched retry budgets to test how additional sampling, reusable task guidance, and failure-label matching affect recovery. DoReMi compares a plan with its execution guo2023doremi . TCoT adds trajectory-level reasoning to a vision-language-action model li2026tcot . Self-correction of reasoning is also unreliable without external feedback, whereas critique grounded in external evidence can help huang2024selfcorrect,gou2024critic . InterCode, AppWorld, and AgentBoard evaluate execution outcomes and intermediate progress yang2023intercode,trivedi2024appworld,ma2024agentboard . With model weights fixed, we ask which information in a robot's retry prompt accounts for recovery. Models receive state information and generate Python programs using a documented robot API, without images. The primary evaluation uses Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct hui2024qwencoder with the primitive API on cube lifting and stacking. An episode comprises an initial program execution for a task and scene, followed by any retries under one method. The initial execution is attempt~0. After an initial failure, the model is allowed up to five retries. Before each retry, the simulator resets to the original scene. Each retry produces a complete program, either generated from scratch or revised from the previous program. We use 252 initial failures for evaluation and 40 for development. This metric measures sequential retries and differs from pass@ estimated from independent samples. For end-to-end studies, initial success is success on attempt~0 and overall success@6 is success in any of the six allowed executions. An attempt is valid if its program compiles, uses only documented API functions, and finishes before timeout. title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
summary: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.

Introduction sec:intro Autonomous driving and ADAS have advanced rapidly over the last decade, driven largely by the availability of large-scale, diverse driving datasets~ nuScenes, kitti, bdd100k, waymo_open_dataset . However, these datasets predominantly capture four-wheeled vehicles operating on well-structured road infrastructure of the Global North. Traffic environments in the Global South present fundamentally different challenges, characterized by unstructured roads, heterogeneous traffic participants, weak lane discipline, and highly dynamic interactions. Although recent datasets such as IDD~ idd and METEOR~ meteor have begun to address these complexities, they continue to focus primarily on four-wheelers. In contrast, Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) are the dominant mode of personal transportation across much of the Global South. The riders are significantly more vulnerable due to minimal physical protection and constant close interactions with other traffic agents. Consequently, MTW users account for a disproportionately large share of road traffic deaths in many countries in the Global South~ morth . Despite their societal importance and elevated safety risks, the community lacks large-scale datasets and standardized benchmarks tailored to understanding the unique challenges of MTW-centric riding. The sensing available on an MTW also differs fundamentally from that assumed by existing driving datasets. MTWs in the Global South are low-cost, high-volume vehicles, and the sensor suites used on four-wheelers, including multi-camera rigs, LiDAR, and differential GNSS, cost a substantial fraction of the vehicle and at times more than the MTW itself. Mounting is equally constrained, as a two-wheeler offers no roof or stable chassis surface, exposes any instrumentation to weather and continuous vibration, and competes directly with rider ergonomics. While richer sensor configurations are feasible for research platforms, a single forward-facing camera remains the only configuration with a realistic path to deployment at scale. Building safe AI systems for MTWs requires the ability to anticipate both the rider's intent and the behavior of surrounding traffic before critical situations unfold. Accordingly, we focus on two complementary predictive perception tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA)~ gebert2019end, jain2015car, jain2016recurrent, khairdoost2020real , which predicts the ego rider's upcoming maneuver from an early portion of the observed video, and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP)~ bitrap, ABC+, PIETraj, SGNet , which forecasts the future 2D bounding-box trajectories of surrounding road agents in the image plane of the rider's ego-centric camera . While recent datasets~ meteor, daad-x have begun investigating predictive tasks in unstructured traffic, they remain focused on four-wheelers. Existing prediction methods are developed for four-wheelers with stable camera viewpoints and structured traffic. These assumptions do not hold for MTWs, which face three key challenges (Fig.~ fig:teaser_fig ). Dynamic ego-motion: unlike rigidly mounted cameras on four-wheelers, MTW-mounted cameras undergo rapid pose and orientation changes due to rider lean, steering corrections and road vibrations, leading to highly non-stationary observations. Weak traffic structure: MTWs frequently navigate narrow gaps and exhibit limited lane adherence in dense mixed traffic, rendering road geometry and lane-based priors unreliable. Contextual occlusion: operating in close proximity to larger vehicles results in persistent, dynamic occlusions that obscure critical cues such as surrounding agents, traffic signals and road boundaries. Collectively, these factors distinguish MTW riding from four-wheeler driving, underscoring the need for datasets and benchmarks tailored to MTW-centric driving in unstructured environments. Despite growing interest in MTW-centric perception, no benchmark exists for predictive perception on motorized two-wheelers. Existing MTW datasets such as MOTOR~ motor support rider action and intention recognition but provide no trajectory annotations for surrounding agents, while trajectory prediction datasets~ chandra2019traphic,meteor focus on four-wheelers. No dataset jointly supports rider maneuver anticipation and surrounding-agent trajectory prediction from an MTW's ego-centric perspective, or characterizes the riding conditions under which prediction is evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce MotoVerse, an MTW-centric predictive benchmark. Our main contributions are as follows: MotoVerse Benchmark. A large-scale ego-centric benchmark for predictive perception on motorized two-wheelers, curated from over 50 hours of collected riding data . MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips and dense trajectory annotations for over surrounding road-agent instances, including more than MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). MTW Challenge Taxonomy. A challenge-aware benchmark annotating three distinctive characteristics of MTW riding: dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling fine-grained evaluation of predictive models under realistic riding conditions. Comprehensive Benchmarking and Insights. Strong baselines for both ERMA and TATP across established conventional prediction models, general-purpose VLMs, and recent driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models , together with a preliminary study of parameter-efficient VLM adaptation, providing the first systematic study of predictive reasoning in MTW-centric unstructured traffic. Related Works sec:lit_survey Datasets Advancing predictive perception in autonomous driving requires datasets that jointly capture rider intentions, surrounding agent motion, and their interactions in realistic traffic environments. This difference also determines the label space, as anticipation requires maneuver classes with identifiable onsets (Sec.~ sec:task_formulation ). Separately, existing MTW datasets provide no trajectory annotations for surrounding traffic participants and therefore cannot support TATP, nor do they provide labels characterizing the riding conditions under which prediction is evaluated. C2D~ C2D aggregates frame-wise features using 2D convolutions, while I3D~ I3D extends convolutional kernels into the temporal dimension for joint spatio-temporal learning. More recent architectures such as SlowFast~ slowfast and X3D~ feichtenhofer2020x3dexpandingarchitecturesefficient improve efficiency through multi-pathway and scalable designs. In the driving domain, maneuver anticipation methods further incorporate temporal models such as LSTMs, transformers, and multi-view perception to predict future driver actions~ gebert2019end, rong2020driver, ma2023cemformer, wasi2024early, daad-x . However, these approaches are primarily developed for four-wheelers equipped with multiple synchronized sensors and cameras. Such hardware configurations are rarely available on MTWs, where a single forward-facing camera remains the most practical sensing modality, and their effectiveness under MTW-specific challenges has not been systematically evaluated. Beyond world and bird's-eye-view formulations~ argoverse2, nuplan , a parallel line of work predicts agent trajectories directly in the image plane of an ego-centric camera, where the output is a future bounding box sequence. Yao ~ fvl introduced this setting for surrounding vehicles; it has since supported accident anticipation~ fol , uncertainty modeling~ bhattacharyya2018longtermonboardpredictionpeople and traffic agent forecasting in risky driving scenarios~ fusiongru . Recent methods such as PIETraj~ PIETraj , SGNet~ SGNet , BiTraP~ bitrap , and action-aware contrastive learning~ ABC+ capture multimodal futures through intention reasoning, goal conditioning, and stochastic prediction. title: METRIC-GS: Selective Metric-Scale Estimation for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: A 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction inherits arbitrary units from structure-from-motion, so it cannot be measured or used to place AR content until someone supplies a scale. Both standard recipes are fragile on real captures: on five indoor scenes with tape-measured ceilings, a quantile floor-to-ceiling heuristic errs by 27% and metric-depth alignment by 35-71% across three networks. We present METRIC-GS, a selective scale estimator for real indoor photographs: it reads the scale off the reconstruction's own semantic content and, just as importantly, refuses when the evidence is thin. A frozen 2D teacher labels Gaussians by visibility-aware voting; instance-level size priors for architectural and furniture classes (doors, tables, the floor-to-ceiling gap) are fused by a robust maximum-likelihood step; and an inlier-mass test turns thin evidence into an explicit abstention that doubles as a router to a heavyweight metric model. On 47 ScanNet++ scenes with laser ground truth, with a configuration frozen before public evaluation, the estimator alone cuts the heuristic's mean error from 21.1% to 16.6% (9.3% on the 28 scenes it acts on) at ~11 s per scene. MASt3R remains the more accurate standalone estimator (9.9%), but routing only our refusals to it matches running it everywhere with 60% fewer invocations; this selective hybrid is the configuration we advocate. Visibility-aware voting raises the scenes the estimator can act on from 16 to 28 at unchanged deployed accuracy. Applied unchanged to 13 phone and drone captures of our own, on which MASt3R fails its own registration gate 12 times, the system improves all five captures it acts on and degrades none. We also report that a current feed-forward metric model scores 2.3% on a benchmark inside its training mixture and 28-35% on captures it has never seen: a published metric-scale number is a best case, not a deployment estimate.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians reconstructs an interior beautifully, but in whatever units structure-from-motion happened to produce. For novel-view synthesis the ambiguity is harmless. The moment the reconstruction has to support a measurement, a robot's path, or an AR object placed at the right size, someone has to supply a scale --- and today that someone is a human with a tape measure. A phone that keeps its inertial stream answers this for free, so the problem belongs to the captures that cannot: DSLR sessions, photo collections, drone surveys, and any pipeline reconstructing from images alone. Two off-the-shelf recipes exist. A geometric heuristic scales the reconstruction so that its floor-to-ceiling extent matches a known room height; a learned alternative aligns SfM depth to a monocular metric-depth network. Both are fragile on real captures: on five indoor scenes with tape-measured ceiling heights, the quantile heuristic errs by 27 on average and metric-depth alignment by 35--71 across three networks, a systematic indoor depth bias rather than one model's flaw; the three networks also disagree with each other by up to a factor of (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Our key observation is that an indoor reconstruction contains many semantic metric anchors (doors, furniture, the floor-to-ceiling gap) whose real-world sizes are standardized or tightly distributed; measured per instance on semantically labeled Gaussians, they over-constrain the global scale. This fixes the operating regime, and we state it upfront: METRIC-GS targets real photographs of indoor scenes whose architecture is visible, with hand-specified size priors drawn from building standards and a frozen 2D segmenter as the only learned component. Outside that regime (outdoor, synthetic appearance, close-ups that never frame a wall) there is nothing to fuse, and the method's contract is to say so rather than to guess. Concretely, a frozen 2D teacher labels Gaussians by projection voting, instance clusters are measured, and a robust maximum-likelihood step fuses the measurements under the size priors (Sec.~ sec:method ). Two design decisions carry the system. First, reliable labeling requires the reconstruction itself: naive projection voting degrades as views are added, because occluded points inherit their occluders' labels. Our visibility-aware voting filters each vote by the model's own rendered depth. Its effect is one of coverage, not accuracy: over all 47 test scenes it lifts the number the estimator can act on from 16 to 28, while the deployed mean error is statistically unchanged (Sec.~ sec:exp-e5 ). Second, an inlier-mass test refuses the correction when too few cues agree, so thin evidence becomes an explicit abstention rather than a confident wrong answer; the same signal routes the scene to a heavyweight metric model. On 47 ScanNet++ scenes with laser-derived metric ground truth, under a configuration frozen before public evaluation, the estimator alone improves the quantile heuristic's mean error from to (median ; Wilcoxon ), reaching on the 28 scenes it acts on at \,s overhead. We are explicit about where the result is strongest: MASt3R is more accurate as a standalone estimator ( ) at over the estimation cost, but on scenes where we act the two are statistically indistinguishable, and routing only our 19 refusals to MASt3R matches running it everywhere with fewer invocations. That selective hybrid, not the standalone accuracy, is the contribution we advocate deploying. Applied unchanged to 13 captures we recorded with consumer phones and a drone, the frozen system improves every capture it acts on, abstains on the rest, and degrades none, while MASt3R fails its own registration gate on 12 of the 13. Our contributions are: a robust fusion of instance-level semantic size cues that reads a metric reference off an indoor reconstruction itself; its measured contribution is robustness, removing the catastrophic failures single-cue estimators cannot defend against; visibility-aware voting, which restricts votes to views that actually observe each Gaussian; it raises the scenes the estimator can act on from 16 to 28 at unchanged deployed accuracy, i.e.\ a coverage gain; abstention as a first-class output: an inlier-mass test that converts insufficient evidence into an explicit refusal and doubles as a router, matching a heavyweight metric model's accuracy at 60 fewer invocations; a measurement worth reporting independently of our estimator: a current feed-forward metric model scores on a benchmark inside its training mixture, on one it was evaluated against, and -- on captures it has never seen; a deployment study under development/test discipline: a configuration frozen before public evaluation, pre-registered held-out predictions, significance tests and negative results, on ScanNet++ (47 scenes), four further public benchmarks, and 13 captures of our own. Related Work sec:related 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3DGS~ kerbl3Dgaussians represents a scene as anisotropic Gaussians optimized with photometric losses and grown by densification heuristics; numerous variants refine its sampling and densification behavior~ mipsplatting, taming3dgs . These heuristics (gradient thresholds, world-size pruning, learning-rate schedules) are expressed in world units, so they silently depend on the arbitrary scale that structure-from-motion~ schoenberger2016sfm assigns to the scene. We make this dependence explicit and turn it into a feature: densification thresholds defined in meters couple scale accuracy to reconstruction quality (Sec.~ sec:method-loop ). Recovering metric scale. Monocular metric depth estimators~ depthanythingv2, metric3d, zoedepth enable a standard alignment recipe: fit a scale (and shift) between predicted depth and SfM depth~ vipe, depthanything3 . We show this recipe carries the depth network's systematic indoor bias (Sec.~ sec:exp-dev ). Feed-forward reconstruction models trained with metric supervision, such as DUSt3R~ dust3r , MASt3R~ mast3r , VGGT~ vggt , and more recently MapAnything~ mapanything and AMB3R~ amb3r , recover impressive metric geometry from images alone, but replace rather than augment an existing SfM/3DGS pipeline, and provide no self-assessment of their scale reliability. We compare empirically to MASt3R's metric checkpoint; MapAnything and AMB3R, its direct successors, are not evaluated here, so the MASt3R error we report is an upper bound on that family's error on curated benchmarks; its successors may do better. Others in this family are explicitly scale-free: ~ pi3 predicts scale-invariant point maps, so a metric anchor of the kind we supply remains necessary downstream. MoGe-2~ moge2 shares our factorization into relative geometry plus a separate global scale, but predicts that scalar from a learned image prior, whereas we read it off the reconstruction's own semantic content, which is what makes an evidence-based refusal possible. Monocular systems have long recovered scale from a geometric anchor such as known object sizes or a ground plane at calibrated camera height~ scaleSLAM, objectSLAM, vgpnav ; a single anchor is precise where it applies but fails when unobserved, whereas we fuse many redundant anchors. Aligning monocular depth priors instead, as HI-SLAM2 does~ hislam2 , imports the depth network's metric bias, which our scale-invariant use of depth avoids. Semantics in 3DGS. Distilling 2D semantics into Gaussians supports open-vocabulary querying and editing~ feature3dgs, langsplat ; structural priors (planes, layout) regularize indoor geometry~ planargs, gsroom, spcgs . These works target geometry quality or semantic access; none address the metric scale. Closest to our voting are LabelGS~ labelgs , which lifts 2D masks with explicit occlusion analysis so occluded Gaussians do not inherit foreground labels, and VALA~ vala , which gates each ray by a Gaussian's marginal contribution. Both address the same pathology, but solve it for segmentation quality. Ours is a cheaper one-sided test against rendered depth, aimed at unbiased instance extents; their finer visibility reasoning is a natural front-end for our partial-instance failure mode. The COLMAP reconstruction it consumes is defined only up to a global scale; our task is to recover that scalar (meters per model unit), or to state explicitly that the evidence does not support one. Deployed error is the scale error of whatever the system returns, active or not. title: USI-Brain: Enhancing Underwater Spatial Intelligence via Spatial Data-Driven Vision-Language Modeling
summary: Underwater spatial reasoning depends on object boundaries and geometric cues that are obscured by scattering, color distortion, and low visibility. Existing underwater resources capture these cues through images, annotations, and depth maps, but provide fragmented supervision for vision-language models. We present a spatial data engine that connects visual appearance with object-level geometry through enhancement, 2D and geometry-assisted question generation, and expert filtering. It produces 4.27M QA pairs across five capability groups. We use this corpus to train USI-Brain and introduce an Underwater Prior-guided Rectifier (UPR) that applies gated corrections to visual features. USI-Bench evaluates the resulting capabilities with 6,525 held-out QA pairs. On its 15 task metrics, USI-Brain and USI-Brain + UPR improve over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct by 5.76 and 7.63 points on average, respectively, using signed differences on 100-point scales. Ablations show that geometry-assisted supervision improves depth and ordering by 4.8 and 6.1 points with UPR disabled, while UPR adds 18.0 points in scene description under matched training data. Both variants use raw images at evaluation. Across NautData, UWBench, and MarineEval, USI-Brain achieves the best or joint-best score on 28 of 32 metrics. Model weights and USI-Bench will be released at https://github.com/SKY-Zhu-91/USI-Brain.

Identifying a structure is one part of this process; determining its position relative to nearby organisms, its visibility, and its spatial extent requires evidence about both appearance and geometry. We study these capabilities as underwater spatial intelligence. Underwater imaging degrades the cues needed for such reasoning. Wavelength-dependent attenuation alters color, while backscatter, blur, and low illumination obscure boundaries and texture akkaynak2019seathru,li2020uieb,gu2023underwatercomputationalimaging . Image enhancement addresses these appearance changes. Questions about depth, ordering, and occlusion additionally require geometric relationships to be represented in the supervision cai2025underwaterdepth . This motivates a data-construction process that combines enhancement with object-linked geometry. The required evidence is distributed across existing resources. NAUTILUS~ xu2025nautilus provides large-scale underwater multimodal data; MarineInst~ zheng2024marineinst , CoralSCOP~ zheng2024coralmask , and SynTIDE~ lin2025syntide contribute instance annotations, segmentation, and depth-related supervision. UWBench~ zhang2025uwbench , CoralVQA~ han2025coralvqa , UQ-Bench~ cao2026uqbench , and MarineEval~ wong2026marineeval evaluate different aspects of underwater understanding. Tables~ tab:train-resource-comparison and~ tab:eval-comparison show the resulting differences in capability coverage. A common QA representation can bring these resources together while retaining the correspondence between an object, its image region, and its geometric cues. Structured spatial supervision has improved general vision-language models in SpatialVLM~ chen2024spatialvlm , Visual Spatial Tuning~ yang2025vst , and OpenSpatial~ liu2026openspatial . We apply this principle to underwater data through a spatial data engine. Hybrid Underwater Enhancement (HUE) prepares images for annotation. A 2D branch generates questions about appearance and image-plane relations; a geometry-assisted branch connects image regions with depth samples and reconstructed object boxes to generate depth, ordering, occlusion, and stratification questions. Capability-based organization and expert review yield 4.27M QA pairs spanning five groups. We train USI-Brain from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct~ bai2025qwen3vl on this corpus. USI-Brain + UPR retains both raw and corrected visual tokens. HUE shapes the training supervision, while UPR operates within the model; both variants are evaluated on raw images. We evaluate the resulting capabilities on USI-Bench, a held-out set of 6,525 QA pairs, and three external benchmarks. GeoQA improves depth and ordering, HUE improves localization and structural perception, and UPR produces its largest incremental gain in scene description.
