Surveys describe the implications of these degradations for underwater perception and computational imaging huy2023underwaterperception,gu2023underwatercomputationalimaging . Underwater depth estimation supplies geometric cues for object placement and scene structure cai2025underwaterdepth . We bring these two sources of information into QA construction: enhancement prepares the visual evidence, and depth or reconstruction links it to object-level spatial relations. Spatial Reasoning Benchmarks and Data Engines. Spatial benchmarks measure object relationships, layouts, and geometric reasoning. Representative datasets include VSR~ liu2023vsr , SpaCE-10~ gong2025space10 , SpatialBench~ xu2025spatialbench , OmniSpatial~ jia2025omnispatial , MM-Spatial~ daxberger2025mmspatial , InternSpatial~ huang2025internspatial , MMSI-Bench~ yang2025mmsi , and TangramPuzzle~ liu2026tangram . Our engine uses object-linked spatial supervision in underwater scenes, combining the available geometric evidence with enhancement during question generation. Underwater Multimodal Models and Resources. NAUTILUS~ xu2025nautilus combines underwater data construction with multimodal model training. OceanGPT~ bi2023oceangpt , OceanGym~ xue2025oceangym , and USIM/U0~ gu2025usimu0 address ocean-domain modeling, evaluation, or embodied interaction. General-purpose backbones such as Qwen3-VL~ bai2025qwen3vl provide a starting point for domain adaptation. title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
summary: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. Since their actions influence future observations, these systems must continually adapt to changing contexts: a robot adjusts its manipulation strategy for different object poses, while a vehicle responds to road and traffic conditions. This continuous feedback makes perception, prediction, and action interdependent~ cosmos3 , making Physical AI consequential for tasks like object handling, spatial navigation, and vehicle operation. Building these capabilities requires exposing systems to diverse environments and interventions, while also testing how they respond when conditions change. Gathering all such experience solely in the real world is costly and can entail risks to people and equipment~ cosmos_v1 . Simulation offers a safe and controllable environment for training, testing, and debugging before deployment. Cosmos world foundation models provide synthetic training data and generate observations for learning in virtual environments~ cosmos_v1,cosmos3 . Learned visual priors expand the range of appearances and scene conditions in these environments, while structured controls retain grounding in the external physical state. As a result, world simulation bridges the gap between data available for learning and the environments needed to evaluate policy behavior. Interactive simulation generates observations incrementally as new controls arrive from a user, a policy, or an external simulator~ gao2026dreamdojo,omnidreams2026 . Evaluating this behavior requires testing how changed controls affect subsequent observations and how well scene changes persist over time. To enable live policy or human interaction at real-world timescales, observations must be returned within the required response time. Achieving this in neural world simulation demands coupling visual generation with control fidelity, retention of state changes, and responsive execution. These requirements motivate transforming a world foundation model into an interactive simulator, while showing that it meets downstream needs still requires independent validation. We introduce a shared post-training framework for converting Cosmos world foundation models into interactive simulators. Built on Cosmos 3~ cosmos3 , the framework adapts broad visual knowledge to predicting how scenes evolve under supplied actions or scene controls. Its purpose is to make that knowledge usable throughout an ongoing interaction, so a user, policy, or external simulator can shape the experience as it unfolds. This supports both learning visual dynamics from recorded experience and generating observations guided by an external simulator's physical state. The framework combines causal training and distillation with streaming execution in a shared recipe for interactive simulation~ zheng2026causalrcm . Post-training teaches the model to follow domain-specific controls and continue from its own generated observations~ huang2025selfforcing . Distillation reduces the computation needed to produce those observations, while streaming execution supports repeated interaction as new inputs become available. Together, these components address visual quality, control fidelity, and timely responses within a common framework. The shared recipe provides a reusable starting point for specialized simulators, with each domain contributing its own controls, data, and evaluation requirements. We ground this approach in three post-trained Cosmos3-Nano model examples: Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual predicts future visual dynamics from a streaming sequence of camera navigation and robot manipulation actions. Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer supports single-view video transfer based on spatial controls, while the state can be maintained externally by a simulator. Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto supports synchronized multi-view AV simulation with LiDAR. All three examples follow the shared procedure, each adapting control representations, data preparation, and modeling choices for its domain. They connect robot interaction, simulator-guided video transfer, and AV scene generation through one post-training framework. Quality, control fidelity, and runtime are evaluated under each example's stated protocols, with policy-driven simulator utility requiring separate closed-loop validation. summarizes this shared foundation and its three post-trained specializations. The technical report is organized as follows. introduces the shared model architecture and its support for simulation controls and causal generation. presents the post-training recipe for causal training and distillation on the foundation model. describes streaming inference optimizations for efficient execution. describe the three model examples, covering their respective architectures, data preparation, training procedures, and evaluation results. discusses related work and concludes the paper. Model Architecture sec::shared_architecture Our framework builds directly on Cosmos 3, retaining its reasoner and generator towers, unified representation space, and positional embedding formulation~ cosmos3 . To support interactive simulation, the architecture must generate observations incrementally as conditioning inputs arrive. The primary shared architectural modification is the introduction of temporal-causal attention across video chunks. This temporal-causal attention ensures that, as each new control becomes available, the simulator predicts subsequent observations autoregressively, without access to future target chunks. During generation, each chunk is produced through iterative denoising, conditioned on both the available observation history and any provided control signals, including language, actions, source video, or structured visual controls. Cosmos 3 Backbone All three example models build directly on Cosmos 3 checkpoints, preserving their multimodal backbone, representation space, and architectural foundations. At the core of Cosmos 3 is a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) design, which organizes processing into two complementary towers: the reasoner and the generator~ deng2025bagel,cosmos3 . Modality-specific encoders and projections first embed each input type ( language, videos, actions) into a shared representation space. Within this architecture, the reasoner tower specializes in autoregressive next-token prediction for language, while the generator tower handles non-language modalities through iterative denoising. MoT towers and joint attention. In each MoT layer, the reasoner and generator towers maintain separate sets of parameters for layer normalization, query/key/value projections, and feed-forward networks. The simulator architecture routes the text prompt into the reasoner tower as the autoregressive subsequence. Visual, control, and denoising-related tokens (including clean conditions, denoised history, and noisy prediction targets) are routed into the generator tower as the diffusion subsequence. Generator queries attend to the entire diffusion subsequence and, via dual-stream joint attention, can also attend to keys and values from the reasoner, while language tokens in the reasoner retain standard causal self-attention. During causal conversion, the generator tower replaces full temporal visibility with temporal-causal attention masking, governed by token role, physical time, and the availability of conditions ( ). Visual encoding and generation. Visual features are extracted by a vision transformer (ViT)~ dosovitskiy2021vit and fed to the reasoner tower, while the generator tower receives latent representations from a causal video variational autoencoder (VAE)~ cosmos3 . A causal RGB tokenizer achieves temporal compression, mapping input frames to latent time steps~ wan2025 . The tokenizer's first latent time step represents the initial RGB frame, and each subsequent step adds 4 RGB frames. Learned projections merge latent patches into the unified representation space. Sampling integrates the output projection's rectified flow velocities into the latents~ liu2023rectifiedflow , and the tokenizer decoder reconstructs RGB observations. For autonomous driving, we extend this design to jointly generate synchronized multi-view RGB videos and LiDAR; see for details. Multimodal positional embedding. Cosmos 3 applies 3D multimodal RoPE (MRoPE)~ bai2025qwen3 to its embeddings, dividing the rotary channels of each attention head among temporal, height, and width coordinates ~ cosmos3 . Within each latent time, both source and target visual tokens share the temporal coordinate , with their spatial coordinates tiling a grid that resets at every frame. Language tokens are encoded with increasing, identical values along all three axes, while action tokens carry temporal positional information and set . A large temporal gap (15,000) separates the autoregressive and diffusion subsequences, and both conditioning and generated visual streams initiate from a common temporal origin. These instantiations inherit the foundation model's MRoPE formulation and maintain the same coordinate offsets throughout causal conversion. Conditioning and control. Cosmos 3 accommodates both language and control streams as direct conditions for video generation~ cosmos3 . Control tokens are concatenated alongside noisy target video tokens and remain clean throughout the denoising of targets. For video transfer, the video tokenizer can process source video or structured visual controls ( depth, segmentation, edges, or blurred videos) to steer generation. In action-conditioned video generation, action tokens express relative camera, end-effector motions, or other transformations. Domain-specific projections adapt action representations of varying dimension into the unified representation~ zheng2026xvla . title: Rohbau3D-Semantics: Dense Semantic and Instance Labels for Point Clouds of Indoor Shell Construction Scenes
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)
summary:
We present the Rohbau3D-Semantics dataset, which adds dense semantic and instance-level labels to laser scans of the previously released Rohbau3D domain data from shell construction sites. The dataset comprises 504 point cloud scenes from 14 survey sites, each captured with a terrestrial laser scanner and stored in a scanner-centered local coordinate system. Unlike point clouds sampled from reconstructed meshes or synthetic building models, the data preserve the characteristic properties of real laser scanning, including non-uniform sampling, measurement artifacts, reflections, and fine geometric detail. Combined with manual labels, expert oversight during pointwise annotation, and full-scene review, this yields a high-quality benchmark for semantic scene understanding in complex built environments. The dataset includes 17 class labels of building components and one background class, along with instance annotations for object-level analysis. In addition to the 3D point clouds, the release also provides scripts for deriving geometrically aligned panoramic and cube-map representations of color, LiDAR reflection intensity, depth, surface normals, semantic labels, and instance labels from the 3D arrays. We describe the acquisition pipeline, annotation protocol, quality-control process, and panorama-generation procedure, and provide benchmark splits and baseline experiments for semantic segmentation. By combining precise terrestrial laser scans, dense annotations, and a wide variety of shell-construction scenes, Rohbau3D-Semantics bridges the gap among synthetic indoor datasets, mesh-derived benchmarks, and smaller construction-specific resources. The dataset is intended to support research on 3D scene understanding, construction-site analytics, and multimodal scene analysis in the built environment.

Introduction sec:intro Spatial scene understanding increasingly depends on benchmark datasets and verified validation data that capture complex environments in faithful digital representations. In recent years, major progress in 3D scene understanding has been driven by large datasets of indoor spaces. However, the individual works primarily focus on furnished residential and office interiors, using synthetic, CAD-derived scenes zheng_Structured3D_2020 , RGB-D reconstructions dai.ScanNet.2017, armeni.Joint.2017 , or high-fidelity laser-scan reconstructions with aligned imagery chandanyeshwanth.ScanNet.2023 . Although these benchmarks have substantially advanced semantic segmentation and related tasks in general, they do not address the actual challenges associated with raw data from terrestrial laser scanners and LiDAR measurements of structural-shell conditions. This limitation is particularly relevant to investigations of shell construction sites. Such scenes are characterized by dynamically changing conditions, temporary structures, stored materials, construction debris, and inconsistent lighting. Fundamental building elements are often unfinished, not yet installed, partially occluded by supporting structures, or concealed by protective coverings. This setting is captured by the German term Rohbau , which denotes the stage of a building project in which only the essential structural shell has been completed. Publicly available datasets for shell construction environments remain scarce, despite the importance of this construction phase for digital documentation and progress monitoring tsige_Automated_2025 , building information modeling (BIM) tang_BIM_2022, chen_Deep_2019 , and quality assurance for building components zhang_Quality_2023 . Resources with dense point-wise semantic and instance annotations for an engineering-based understanding of the framework structure are rarer still rauch.Semantic.2023 . Such annotations are particularly valuable in construction settings because many downstream tasks require not only recognizing object categories, but also distinguishing individual elements. While semantic labels support the identification of structurally relevant classes, instance-level annotations are essential for object-wise analysis, such as tracking the installation state of individual components zou_Method_2025 , comparing as-built conditions against BIM models tsige_Automated_2025, macher_Point_2015 , localizing defects, or reasoning about navigable and obstructed space feng_Integration_2026 . To address this gap, we present Rohbau3D-Semantics, an extension of the previously released Rohbau3D dataset rauch_Rohbau3D_2025 . The original Rohbau3D release provided terrestrial laser scans and associated metadata from diverse shell construction sites, but no semantic annotations. Rohbau3D-Semantics extends the raw data with point-wise labels, aligned 2D panoramic projections, benchmark splits, and baseline results for supervised 3D semantic segmentation. The instance labels and linked 2D representations are released to support future instance-level and multimodal research, but these tasks are not evaluated in the present experiments. Although rooted in the construction domain, the dataset may also be relevant to broader work in automation and robotics involving cluttered or structurally degraded built environments le_3D_2025, pan_Postdisaster_2025 . Related Datasets sec:related_data While several datasets support indoor 3D scene understanding, none captures the same technical scope of shell construction sites. ScanNet v2 dai.ScanNet.2017 and S3DIS armeni.3D.2016 are central real-world indoor benchmarks based on RGB-D reconstructions or registered point samples. ScanNet++ chandanyeshwanth.ScanNet.2023 adds high-end laser scans, DSLR images, and iPhone RGB-D sequences. These datasets, however, primarily depict completed, furnished interiors rather than scanner-centered raw terrestrial scans of unfinished structural shells. Structured3D zheng_Structured3D_2020 provides virtual indoor scenes rendered from CAD models, while VASAD langlois.VASAD.2022 samples synthetic point clouds from digital building models. Although useful for scalable training, their point distributions arise from rendering or sampling rather than physical sensing. LiDAR-Net guo_LiDARNet_2024 instead supplies real, unfiltered mobile-LiDAR data with uneven density, noise, and registration errors, but its taxonomy mainly describes common architectural elements and furnishings rather than components specific to structural shells. Public construction-site data remains scarce. Hilti-Oxford lintongzhang.HiltiOxford.2022 and ConSLAM m.trzeciak_ConSLAM_2022 combine cameras, LiDAR, and inertial sensing in construction environments, but target SLAM, registration, or progress monitoring and provide no semantic annotations sun_Nothing_2023 . ConSite yue.ConSite.2026 has recently provided TLS data with semantic labels for 13 classes of structural and temporal components, though without instance annotations and only on a small scale. Table tab:dataset_comparison makes the different dataset roles explicit: mobile construction-site datasets target localization and mapping without semantic or instance labels, whereas ConSite provides construction-specific semantic labels but no instances. Against this background, Rohbau3D-Semantics combines real construction-site data with point-wise semantic and instance annotations and linked 2D representations. Among the compared site-related datasets with explicitly reported annotated point totals, it provides the largest collection, with 504 standalone scans and 12.5 billion points. Dataset Description dataset_overview Rohbau3D-Semantics builds upon the previously published Rohbau3D dataset, in which the underlying terrestrial laser scans were released as point clouds under a CC BY 4.0 license~ rauch_Rohbau3D_2025 . The present work extends these data with dense point-wise semantic and instance annotations and a reproducible pipeline for deriving corresponding panoramic and cube-map representations. The original publication documents the data acquisition and preprocessing in detail. For completeness, this section summarizes the relevant processing steps before describing the new annotation workflow and the resulting dataset. Data Collection and Processing The source data were collected over a 1-year period at multiple construction sites in the Munich area, Germany. The survey sites were selected in collaboration with four construction companies and the Munich State Building Authority to ensure diversity in building typologies, construction conditions, and the occurrence of objects. As a result, the dataset covers a broad range of unfinished indoor environments, with varying surface materials, architectural features, and stages of construction progress visible. All point clouds were acquired using a steady FARO Focus M70 terrestrial laser scanner shown in Figure fig:scanner_setup . This device can capture up to 1 million spherical points per second using LiDAR technology and produce colored point clouds by superimposing spherical high-dynamic-range (HDR) images in post-processing. Construction management and supervision use comparable business-grade laser scanners to measure, document, and evaluate ongoing construction processes. The laser scanner is tripod-mounted, which improves measurement quality compared to handheld devices. This setup yields high point density, high geometric accuracy, and consistent acquisition results, while preserving characteristic sensing imperfections, such as occlusions, reflections, and measurement artifacts, as illustrated in Figure fig:reflections . Scan positions were selected individually on site by a trained civil engineer to mimic the process of creating as-built documentation. The individual scans were not registered into a common global coordinate frame. Instead, each scan is stored in its local scanner-centered coordinate system, with the sensor origin located at in the world coordinate system. This representation ensures a consistent, standardized structure across all samples, and a frame-like field of view, comparable to that of mobile LiDAR devices. Preprocessing was intentionally kept minimal to preserve the raw measurement characteristics. The only geometric filtering step removed points located outside a sphere of radius 25\,m centered at the scanner origin to suppress unstable long-range measurements. No resampling, mesh reconstruction, or geometric regularization was applied. Consequently, the dataset retains the irregular sampling pattern and sensor-specific artifacts of LiDAR sensing, which pose a key challenge for 3D data analysis of actual sensor data rauch_Rohbau3D_2025 . Site descriptions and file-format details are provided in the supplementary material; scene-wise feature compendia are available in the dataset repository~ rauch_Rohbau3D_2026 . Data Annotation The proposed Rohbau3D-Semantics dataset uses a semantic taxonomy of 17 foreground classes and one background class. The class set was defined as a condensed selection of object categories that are both relevant to building information modeling (BIM) and exist frequently enough in the data to be represented as independent classes. This design avoids overly fine-grained labels for rare objects while taking into account the important components for modeling the building. The list of annotation classes defines: (0) None, (01) Ceiling, (02) Slanted Ceiling, (03) Ceiling Cutout, (04) Floor, (05) Wall, (06) Drywall, (07) Wall Cutout, (08) Parapet, (09) Beam, (10) Column, (11) Staircase, (12) Window Cutout, (13) Window, (14) Door Rough Opening, (15) Facade Element, (16) Elevator Doors, and (17) TGA (technical building equipment), often referred to as mechanical electrical plumbing (MEP). title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.

Introduction sec:intro Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) is an effective paradigm for generalizable novel view synthesis. Given a set of calibrated images, recent methods directly predict an explicit Gaussian representation in a single forward pass~ pixelsplat,mvsplat,depthsplat , avoiding scene-specific optimization while retaining the efficient rendering properties of 3D-GS~ 3dgs . However, as feed-forward reconstruction expands from sparse observations to longer sequences, both the reconstructed representation and the cross-view computation used to construct it become increasingly difficult to scale. A model that is efficient for a few input images may therefore become impractical when processing tens or hundreds of views. Recent methods~ freesplat,zpressor have begun to address the issue of scaling in representation size. For instance, ZPressor~ zpressor partitions the input images into a fixed number of groups using camera poses. It selects one anchor view from each group and fuses the remaining support views into the corresponding anchor feature maps. Only these updated anchor features are passed to the pixel-aligned Gaussian decoder. Since the number of anchor views remains constant, adding additional support views to provide further scene information does not directly increase the input to the Gaussian decoder or the number of Gaussians. This divide-and-conquer strategy, however, introduces a new scaling dilemma. Increasing the number of camera groups reduces the support burden per anchor, but also increases the number of decoder-facing anchors and generated Gaussians. Keeping the anchor set fixed instead preserves representation size while forcing each anchor to aggregate an increasing number of support views. This exposes a growing support-to-anchor fusion bottleneck even though the decoder-facing representation remains fixed. We refer to this contradiction as the representation--fusion mismatch: bounding the decoder-facing anchor representation does not bound the support evidence required to construct it. As more views are assigned to a fixed set of anchors, the representation remains compact while support-side K/V projection and cross-attention continue to grow. Token reduction offers a direct way to reduce this cost. Learned methods adapt token selection to individual inputs and tasks~ dynamicvit,spvit,tokencropr , but typically require task-specific training or fine-tuning. When inserted into a feed-forward reconstruction pipeline, such modules may also require the host model to be jointly adapted, which is particularly costly for generalizable 3D-GS models trained on large-scale multi-view data. We therefore focus on inference-time reduction that can be applied directly to released checkpoints. Training-free methods~ tome,optin,zerotprune prune or merge redundant visual tokens, while Spark3R~ spark3r shows that K/V tokens can often tolerate stronger reduction than queries. In anchor-based fusion, however, the decoder-facing queries are already bounded by construction. The remaining challenge is to control the growing support-side K/V sequence while preserving evidence from all support views. We therefore introduce , a training-free method for scalable cross-view fusion in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. constrains the growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing: it assigns different spatial sampling offsets across support views and varies them across fusion layers, so additional views contribute evidence without proportionally increasing the K/V sequence. Routing is applied before K/V projection, and routed contexts are packed jointly across fusion layers. The original camera grouping, anchor representation, attention modules, and Gaussian decoder remain unchanged. Our main contributions are: We identify the representation--fusion mismatch: bounding the decoder-facing representation does not prevent support-to-anchor fusion from growing with the number of views. We propose with coverage-cycled evidence routing, which bounds the support-side sequence while distributing spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers. We route support features before K/V projection, reducing both support-side projection and attention cost without retraining. Experiments across multiple backbones and datasets demonstrate strong long-context acceleration while maintaining reconstruction quality. Related Work sec:related Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS)~ 3dgs represents a scene using explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives and enables high-quality novel-view rendering through an efficient differentiable rasterizer. While the standard approach~ 3dgs relies on scene-by-scene optimization to generate a separate set of Gaussian parameter representations for each scene, feed-forward methods ~ pixelsplat,mvsplat,mvsgaussian,c3gs,depthsplat,monosplat directly predict scene representations from input images and thereby support novel-view synthesis without scene-specific optimization. This feed-forward paradigm is inspired by previous neural rendering methods~ pixelnerf,ibrnet,mvsnerf . These generalizable NeRF models are also capable of performing novel-view synthesis based on features extracted from input images, without requiring per-scene optimization. PixelSplat~ pixelsplat predicts pixel-aligned Gaussians from sparse image pairs. MVSplat~ mvsplat further incorporates plane-sweep cost volumes and cross-view feature aggregation for geometric reconstruction, following the broader use of multi-view correspondence reasoning in learning-based MVS~ mvsnet,casmvsnet,patchmatchnet,geomvsnet,icg-mvsnet,hu20223d . DepthSplat~ depthsplat additionally integrates pretrained monocular depth features to strengthen geometric reasoning and cross-dataset generalization. This type of pixel-aligned method suffers from an inherent issue: the number of decoded Gaussians increases with the number of input viewpoints, as additional viewpoint-aligned feature maps lead to the prediction of more Gaussian primitives. ZPressor~ zpressor reduces representation growth by compressing multiple input views into a compact set of decoder-facing anchor features. However, its support-to-anchor fusion still processes view-growing support evidence, so the cost of constructing the retained representation continues to increase with the number of input views. Our work is complementary to this representation compression. keeps the original anchor representation and downstream Gaussian prediction pipeline unchanged, while making the support-to-anchor fusion more scalable. Visual Token Reduction Token reduction has been extensively studied for accelerating Vision Transformers~ vit . One class of methods learns input- or task-dependent token selection policies jointly with the model. For example, DynamicViT~ dynamicvit learns lightweight prediction modules for dynamic token sparsification, while more recent methods such as Token Cropr~ tokencropr learn task-aware token retention through auxiliary prediction objectives. Such learned reduction can adapt to the target task, but generally requires additional training or fine-tuning, and therefore does not directly preserve compatibility with existing reconstruction checkpoints. Training-free methods instead modify token processing at inference time. Adaptive Token Sampling (ATS)~ ats performs parameter-free sampling using attention responses, but the attention information used for filtering must first be obtained. ToMe~ tome merges similar tokens through bipartite matching, while Zero-TPrune~ zerotprune performs zero-shot token pruning without retraining. These methods provide general-purpose mechanisms for reducing visual tokens, but do not explicitly address how multi-view evidence should be distributed when many support cameras jointly construct a fixed decoder-facing representation. Spark3R~ spark3r also studies training-free asymmetric token reduction for feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods~ vggt,depthanything3 and observes that Key/Value tokens can often be reduced more aggressively than queries. The scenario we address concerns a different type of bottleneck. In ZPressor-style anchor fusion, the decoder-facing anchor queries are already bounded by design, while the support evidence used to construct these queries continues to grow with the number of input views. summary: While recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods enable efficient driving-scene reconstruction from surround-view images, their reliance on a single observation fundamentally hinders novel-view synthesis. Regions occluded in the input can become visible from novel viewpoints, leaving the reconstructed Gaussians under-constrained and incomplete. Moving beyond image-space inpainting for rendered views, we introduce OccSplat, a feed-forward framework whose core contribution is Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification, explicitly targeting missing scene geometry rather than missing pixels. By predicting new Gaussian primitives for unsupported regions, OccSplat completes the scene directly in the 3D representation. Specifically, OccSplat first identifies occluded regions that lack Gaussian support through Gaussian Occlusion Mapping. Gaussian Occlusion Completion then generates new primitives for these regions. The predicted primitives are integrated into the original representation to improve novel-view synthesis while retaining feed-forward inference without per-scene optimization. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that OccSplat improves on the compared methods and yields particularly large gains in occluded regions, leading to more accurate and visually coherent driving-scene reconstruction.

Introduction sec:intro Photorealistic reconstruction and novel-view synthesis of driving scenes from vehicle-mounted cameras are foundational capabilities for autonomous driving, underpinning closed-loop simulation, safe evaluation of perception and planning stacks, and large-scale data augmentation for rare or safety-critical events. The recent emergence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs , which represents a scene with an explicit set of anisotropic Gaussians and renders through fast differentiable rasterization, enables fast, high-fidelity rendering after scene optimization and has become a widely used representation for this setting. Building on 3DGS, a growing body of work specializes the representation to driving scenes~ zhou2024drivinggaussian,yan2024street,huang2024textit,khan2025autosplat , modeling the static background, dynamic actors, and unbounded street layout that characterize on-road data. These methods achieve impressive rendering quality, but are fundamentally per-scene optimization approaches: each scene must be fit individually, typically requiring densely overlapping views, accurate camera extrinsics, and minutes to hours of optimization. The need to optimize each new scene limits throughput in large-scale autonomous-driving pipelines. To lift these constraints, feed-forward (generalizable) Gaussian Splatting predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives directly from images in a single forward pass, enabling training on large corpora and inference without per-scene optimization on unseen scenes~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,chen2024mvsplat360,huang2025no,kang2025selfsplat,szymanowicz2024splatter,xu2025depthsplat,ye2025no,zhang2024gs . DrivingForward~ tian2025drivingforward adapts this paradigm to driving, jointly learning pose, depth, and Gaussian networks in a self-supervised manner so that surround-view scenes can be reconstructed without depth ground truth or camera extrinsics. We focus on its challenging single-frame (SF) setting: the model observes only the surround-view images of the current frame and must synthesize the surround views of the future frame . As the ego-vehicle drives forward between and , the camera rig translates along the direction of travel and the effective viewpoint changes. Consequently, scene regions that are occluded at , hidden behind trees, poles, fences, or building edges, become disoccluded at (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Feed-forward pixel-aligned methods place a Gaussian only where there is an observed pixel to lift it from, so surfaces with no visible support at receive no primitives at all. When these surfaces are exposed at , the renderer has nothing to draw in their place, yielding holes and stretched ``rubber-sheet'' artifacts. This disocclusion gap is intrinsic to forward-driving SF synthesis: it arises from viewpoint changes that reveal content absent from the source images. Quo vadis? Where, then, is the scene going? The question is literal as well as rhetorical: the model must reason not only about what it currently sees, but about the content that its forward motion is about to uncover. We therefore recast future-frame driving reconstruction as an Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification problem and instantiate it in OccSplat, a feed-forward surround-view framework that anticipates and completes soon-to-be-revealed content before the ego-vehicle uncovers it. Starting from a pixel-aligned Gaussian representation of the current frame, OccSplat first localizes regions that lack Gaussian support and are therefore prone to disocclusion, then densifies them with new 3D Gaussian primitives that plausibly complete the disoccluded geometry and appearance. Because these primitives are fused into the same representation as the observed scene, the completed content can be rendered from a shared 3D representation instead of being patched independently in each image. This densification is a single additional feed-forward pass on top of the backbone, closing the disocclusion gap while retaining feed-forward inference without per-scene optimization. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce OccSplat, a feed-forward framework that reframes occlusion handling as Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification, targeting missing scene geometry rather than missing pixels by predicting new Gaussian primitives for occluded regions. We design two modules realizing this idea: Gaussian Occlusion Mapping, which identifies regions lacking Gaussian support, and Gaussian Occlusion Completion, which generates and integrates new primitives for them. Extensive experiments on nuScenes show that OccSplat improves on the compared feed-forward methods, with particularly large gains in occluded regions. Related Work sec:Related Work Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. To eliminate the expensive per-scene optimization of conventional 3DGS, numerous feed-forward approaches have been proposed to directly predict Gaussian representations from sparse input images. Early methods such as PixelSplat charatan2024pixelsplat and Splatter Image szymanowicz2024splatter generate Gaussians from image features, while MVSplat chen2024mvsplat and DepthSplat xu2025depthsplat improve geometric reconstruction through explicit cross-view matching and geometry-aware representations. Subsequent methods~ ye2025no, jiang2025anysplat, zhang2025flare, ye2025yonosplat , further relax pose requirements and enable reconstruction in pose-free or fully uncalibrated settings. Despite their impressive efficiency and generalization ability, these methods often struggle in sparse-view scenarios with severe occlusions and limited view overlap, resulting in incomplete geometry and inconsistent scene representations. Driving Scene Reconstruction. NeRFs~ mildenhall2021nerf and 3DGS~ 3dgs have been adapted to driving scene reconstruction~ zhou2024drivinggaussian, yan2024street, huang2024textit, khan2025autosplat . However, most of them focus on high-quality reconstruction of individual scenes, relying on offline per-scene optimization, which limits their applicability to online driving systems. Their reconstruction quality can also degrade under severe occlusions and sparse-view observations. A few recent feed-forward and pose-free approaches, such as ye2025no, smart2024splatt3r, jiang2025anysplat, zhang2025flare , explore online reconstruction for driving scenes, but they mainly focus on general scene reconstruction and cross-scene generalization, while lacking explicit mechanisms for handling severe occlusions and sparse-view ambiguities. DistillNeRF wang2024distillnerf proposes a generalizable framework for driving scenes and achieves reasonable novel view synthesis, but it requires an expensive offline NeRF optimization stage per scene and additional LiDAR supervision, while still struggling in highly occluded regions. In contrast, OccSplat targets feed-forward driving scene reconstruction from RGB inputs alone while improving robustness to occlusions and incomplete observations in sparse-view environments. Occlusion-aware and Structure-aware 3DGS. Recent efforts have sought to improve structural modeling and visibility reasoning in 3DGS. Scaffold-GS lu2024scaffold introduces an anchor-based representation to enhance structural control and reconstruction efficiency, while CityGaussian liu2024citygaussian and Octree-GS ren2024octree improve scalability through hierarchical scene representations. OccluGaussian liu2025occlugaussian further enhances reconstruction consistency by leveraging occlusion-aware scene partitioning based on camera co-visibility. In parallel, methods for recovering missing or occluded regions~ dahaghin2025splatfill, huang20253d, zhou2025high, shi2025imfine employ depth-guided geometry reasoning, multi-view consistency constraints, and iterative refinement to recover incomplete scene content. However, these methods still rely on scene-specific optimization and therefore cannot operate in a fully feed-forward manner. Method sec:method Overview sec:overview Given the surround-view images of the current frame , OccSplat aims to synthesize the surround views of the future frame while completing the scene content that the ego-vehicle's forward motion will disocclude. As shown in Fig.~ fig:architecture , our pipeline builds on a feed-forward surround-view backbone and augments it with two occlusion-handling modules that operate directly on the Gaussian representation. Because is generated only from pixels observed at , it provides no support for surfaces occluded in the current frame. As the viewpoint advances, these hidden regions become visible, yet the renderer lacks the primitives needed to synthesize them, producing structural holes, stretched surfaces, and appearance inconsistencies. OccSplat closes this gap in two steps that operate directly on . title: Uncertainty-Driven Efficient Communication for UAV-Based Collaborative Perception
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based collaborative perception enables multiple agents to share complementary perceptual information, overcoming limitations such as occlusion and limited sensing range. Communication efficiency is a critical bottleneck, as UAVs operate under stringent bandwidth and computational constraints. However, existing spatial selection methods focus predominantly on foreground regions to reduce missed detections, neglecting perceptually ambiguous regions and leaving false detections unresolved. We propose UCP, an uncertainty-driven framework that characterizes collaborative value through observational uncertainty, identifying sensor-limited regions, and discriminative uncertainty, capturing model-level ambiguity near the decision boundary. These estimates drive spatial request and supply maps for efficient inter-agent communication, and the received messages are aggregated via U-Fusion, an uncertainty-guided cross-attention module. Experiments on three benchmarks across 3D object detection and trajectory prediction demonstrate a superior performance-bandwidth trade-off with high interpretability and strong generalizability.

title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Streaming video understanding requires models to interpret an evolving visual world and interact while observations are still arriving~ chen2024videollmonline,qian2025dispider,zeng2026onestreamer . Unlike offline video understanding~ zhang2024llavavideo , where the complete video is available before answering, streaming interaction unfolds through repeated decisions under partial observations. At each turn, a model must decide whether to respond or continue observing~ wang2024mmduet,wang2025mmduet2 . A useful assistant should respond when new evidence warrants an answer, provide follow-up information when needed, and remain silent when another reply would add little value. The appropriate action therefore depends not only on the current visual evidence~ dong2026interleaved,guo2026beyond,yu2026mact , but also on what the model has already communicated. Learning this sequence of response and waiting decisions requires feedback that reflects answer quality and interaction timing. Reinforcement learning~ sutton2018reinforcement,schulman2017ppo,shao2024deepseekmath,dong2026rl provides a natural way to learn these decisions from interaction-level feedback, with recent approaches adopting Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~ shao2024deepseekmath . MMDuet2~ wang2025mmduet2 optimizes proactive interaction with PAUC-based rewards~ wang2025proactivevideoqa , while ThinkStream~ liu2026thinkstream combines incremental reasoning with rewards for correctness, format, and response timing. StreamPro~ li2026streampro further incorporates both turn-level and trajectory-level rewards to assess individual responses and overall interaction quality. Reward design and short-span training~ wang2025mmduet2 improve interaction feedback, but the trajectory-level GRPO formulations considered here still broadcast one advantage across decision turns. Turn-level scoring and turn-specific policy credit are therefore distinct design choices. A good trajectory can contain bad turns, and a bad trajectory can contain good turns. After a successful early response, a redundant reply may still inherit a positive trajectory advantage, even if the reward penalizes repetition ( ). Conversely, a useful follow-up after earlier failures may receive a negative advantage because the trajectory remains below the group average. In both cases, rewards accrued before the current decision influence its learning signal, potentially obscuring the value of responding or waiting at that turn. We therefore argue that a streaming decision's learning signal should emphasize the return from that turn onward, rather than rewards accumulated earlier. Guided by this principle, we propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns advantage estimation and loss aggregation with streaming decisions. Building on the return-to-go principle~ sutton2018reinforcement , TurnWise exploits the explicit waiting action to score each trajectory prefix with all remaining turns set to silence. Subtracting this prefix reference from the full trajectory reward yields a remaining return, from which we construct group-relative, turn-specific advantages. Silence-completed prefix scoring converts trajectory feedback into turn-specific remaining-return advantages. The computation reuses existing rollout evaluations, requiring neither a learned critic nor additional rollouts. TurnWise couples turn-specific credit with equal weighting of response and waiting decisions. Under token-mean aggregation, longer responses still receive larger aggregation weights than short waiting actions. We therefore introduce turn-mean loss aggregation, averaging token losses within each turn before averaging across turns within each trajectory. Turn-mean aggregation balances sampled response and waiting decisions directly in the RL objective, making each turn's weight independent of its output length. Together, the two designs make the decision turn a common unit for advantage estimation and loss aggregation, addressing both how a turn receives credit and how its feedback is weighted during policy optimization. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We identify a granularity mismatch in streaming video RL. Shared trajectory advantages can obscure the value of later decisions, while token-mean loss aggregation makes turn weights depend on response length. We introduce TurnWise, combining silence-completed prefix scoring for turn-specific remaining-return advantages with turn-mean loss aggregation, without a learned critic or additional rollouts. We achieve the best aggregate scores on ProactiveVQA~ wang2025proactivevideoqa , OVO-Timing~ niu2025ovobench , and StreamingBench~ lin2026streamingbench with both Qwen backbones, and show that turn-mean aggregation improves response timing while reducing repetition relative to credit-only optimization. Related Work sec:related Streaming Video Interaction Streaming video interaction extends offline video understanding~ zhang2024llavavideo by requiring models to process incoming observations and decide when to communicate. Unlike answering after viewing an entire video, these models must operate on observed prefixes and accommodate evolving user queries. VideoLLM-online~ chen2024videollmonline introduces online video-language modeling, while MMDuet~ wang2024mmduet broadens time-sensitive comprehension through interleaved video-text dialogue. Dispider~ qian2025dispider disentangles perception, decision, and reaction, and StreamBridge~ wang2025streambridge equips offline models with a lightweight proactive activation module. TimeChat-Online~ yao2025timechatonline reduces visual redundancy, while Flash-VStream~ zhang2025flashvstream maintains compact memory for real-time understanding of long video streams. Streamo~ xia2026streamo further supports diverse streaming tasks through large-scale instruction tuning, including narration, event captioning, and time-sensitive question answering. Benchmarks including ProactiveVideoQA~ wang2025proactivevideoqa , OVO-Bench~ niu2025ovobench , and StreamingBench~ lin2026streamingbench cover real-time perception, historical understanding, and proactive response timing. These studies establish the setting for learning response and waiting decisions, while our work focuses on how RL feedback is assigned and weighted across those decisions. Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding PPO~ schulman2017ppo and GRPO~ shao2024deepseekmath provide widely used foundations for language-model policy optimization. Their application to video models has progressed from preference alignment to temporal reasoning and long-video training. VLM-RLAIF~ ahn2024vlmrlaif uses AI-generated feedback for video instruction tuning. Video-R1~ feng2025videor1 encourages temporal reasoning through T-GRPO, VideoChat-R1~ li2025videochatr1 strengthens spatio-temporal perception through reinforcement fine-tuning, and LongVILA-R1~ chen2025scalingrl scales RL training to long video inputs. Policy distillation can improve initialization for subsequent RL~ dong2026rl,yu2026dopd . In streaming settings, MMDuet2~ wang2025mmduet2 optimizes PAUC-based interaction rewards and uses short-span training to mitigate reward sparsity and temporal credit assignment. ThinkStream~ liu2026thinkstream trains incremental reasoning with accuracy, format, and timing rewards, while StreamPro~ li2026streampro combines turn-level response scores with trajectory-level coherence rewards. These approaches improve evaluation of sampled interactions, but their trajectory-level GRPO formulations derive a shared advantage from the aggregated reward. TurnWise aligns streaming policy optimization with decision turns through group-relative remaining-return credit and turn-mean loss aggregation. title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management
comment: Accepted by IEEE AP-GARSS 2026; 4 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench. Multimodal Large Language Models, Training-free Method, Remote Sensing, Urban Management. INTRODUCTION Remote sensing (RS) has become an important information source for urban management, supporting a range of applications, including urban sustainability monitoring, disaster risk management, and observation of diverse urban environments kadhim2016advances, ghaffarian2018remote, chen2024remote . In these applications, effective image understanding should not stop at scene-level recognition, but should support task-specific reasoning based on fine-grained visual evidence jiang2025eaglevision, li2026provg . Since such reasoning tasks are often task-dependent and difficult to cover with a fixed set of predefined labels, MLLMs offer a flexible interface for interpreting RS images through natural-language queries and linking fine-grained visual evidence to task-specific reasoning. However, fine-grained visual reasoning in urban management remains underexplored in MLLM evaluation. Existing RS evaluation benchmarks primarily focus on scene-level visual capabilities li2024vrsbench . However, models may rely on scene-level priors, inferring answers from overall scene context or common object co-occurrence rather than from fine-grained visual evidence, a failure mode related to object hallucination in vision-language models li2023evaluating . For example, scene-level questions may ask whether an image contains a road, while fine-grained questions ask whether a vehicle crosses a lane line or whether local cracks exist. Traditional datasets, such as RSVQA lobry2020rsvqa , mainly evaluate scene classification or generic question answering, where many answers can be inferred from scene-level information without explicitly testing fine-grained visual evidence. Even high-resolution benchmarks, such as FloodNet rahnemoonfar2021floodnet , primarily evaluate scene classification or generic question answering, focusing on scene-level understanding or binary classification. Existing evaluations rarely test the intersection of fine-grained visual inspection and logical reasoning. In real-world RS applications, targets can be minute, ambiguous, and embedded in complex backgrounds. Current evaluations do not test whether an MLLM discerns these fine-grained visual details or guesses from scene-level priors. To address this gap, we introduce UMBench, an Urban Management Benchmark for fine-grained visual reasoning in complex RS scenarios. It is built from 583 UAV images and contains 2,733 expert-curated QA pairs spanning traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. UMBench tests whether models can combine fine-grained visual inspection with reasoning instead of relying on scene-level priors. To reduce reliance on scene-level priors, we propose a training-free evidence-first chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting method wei2022chain . The method guides models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence before making a final choice. Since it requires no model fine-tuning or access to model weights, it can be applied to both open-source MLLMs and commercial MLLMs. Experiments on representative Qwen-VL, InternVL, and commercial models show that the proposed method improves performance across different access settings. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. We propose UMBench, the first urban remote sensing benchmark for fine-grained visual reasoning in urban management. We design a novel training-free method to guide MLLMs to focus on fine-grained visual evidence rather than scene-level priors. The designed method is applicable to both open-source and commercial MLLMs due to its training-free property. UMBENCH DATASET In this work, fine-grained visual reasoning denotes questions that cannot be solved from a global scene category alone. A correct answer must be supported by fine-grained evidence, including small-object inspection, attribute judgment, spatial-relation reasoning, or explicit verification against a plausible scene-level prior. This distinction is important for urban management because visually similar scenes may encode different operational states, such as lawful traffic versus lane crossing, intact pavement versus local cracking, or normal water surfaces versus inundation. UMBench comprises 583 UAV images covering urban environments, complementing large-scale RS vision-language resources zhang2023rs5m, liu2024remoteclip . The processed images are stored in PNG format, with the longer side resized to 800 pixels while preserving aspect ratio; GSD metadata was not available from the processed files. The image pool includes intersections, parking lots, residential blocks, construction zones, rivers, parks, green spaces, and open fields. Rather than treating high pixel resolution as the primary contribution, UMBench emphasizes task-relevant evidence such as vehicles, lane markings, barriers, pavement texture, water surfaces, vegetation patterns, and object relations. Blurred, overexposed, ambiguous, and near-duplicate images were removed during quality control. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:dataset_overview , the benchmark organizes 2,733 QA pairs into four application groups: Traffic Monitoring evaluates vehicle behavior, congestion, parking use, and lane relations; Urban Construction examines buildings, roads, and construction conditions; Environmental Quality covers water, vegetation, waste, and air-quality evidence; and Disaster Warning targets inundation, collapse, fire, obstruction, and infrastructure risks. A QA pair may receive multiple application tags, yielding 3,305 cumulative tag assignments (TM/UC/EQ/DW: 1,129/755/992/429). Each instance is a multiple-choice question designed to resist answers based on scene-level priors. Annotators first identified a visually verifiable evidence region, formulated a question whose answer depends on that region, and then constructed scene-compatible distractors that differ in fine-grained visual evidence. All QA pairs were manually curated and reviewed by an expert team for visual verifiability, distractor plausibility, and ambiguity. Disagreements were resolved through consensus discussion, and ambiguous cases with unclear evidence or multiple plausible answers were revised or removed. Since labels were finalized through consensus-based expert curation, we report this quality-control protocol rather than an independent inter-annotator agreement score. The complete set is reserved for zero-shot evaluation without task-specific training. EVIDENCE-FIRST COT METHOD As discussed, current MLLMs may rely on scene-level priors when analyzing complex remote sensing imagery, allowing macroscopic context to override fine-grained visual evidence. Inspired by CoT and multimodal reasoning prompts wei2022chain, zhang2023multimodalcot , we propose a lightweight, training-free evidence-first Chain-of-Thought prompting method. Instead of asking the model to reason freely, the method imposes an explicit evidence bottleneck: the model must first ground the question in visible local cues, then suppress scene-level priors, and finally map the verified evidence to a constrained option. This ordering is designed for UMBench, where distractors are often semantically plausible at the scene level but inconsistent with small visual details. This design can be viewed as a compact verify-then-answer framework, as summarized in Fig.~ fig:prompt_framework . It requires no fine-tuning or access to model weights, and can therefore be applied to both open-source and commercial models. The framework contains three modules. Visual Grounding asks the model to inspect local objects, attributes, and spatial relations before using high-level semantics. Prior Suppression weakens answers supported only by scene type or common co-occurrence patterns. Standardized Output constrains the response to a final option letter, making evaluation robust to verbose outputs. The ordered stages prevent a fluent but unsupported conclusion from bypassing visual verification. Because the image, options, decoding configuration, and model parameters remain unchanged, the method isolates the effect of evidence-oriented prompting without introducing additional supervision or task-specific training. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS Experimental Setup We evaluate MLLMs under two complementary access settings. In the local setting, three compact open-source models are deployed under the same preprocessing and inference environment, providing a reproducible test of the method on resource-conscious systems. In the cloud setting, three commercial models are queried without access to their weights, testing whether the same prompt-level intervention transfers to black-box services. All experiments are zero-shot and use identical images, questions, options, and decoding settings across models; only the prompting instruction changes. All models receive the processed PNG images without red-box annotations: local models use their official image processors and default visual-token settings, while commercial models receive the same images through provider APIs. We use fixed decoding settings when available and report exact top-1 accuracy on the full benchmark. Outputs without a valid final option are counted as incorrect. We additionally compare direct answering with standard zero-shot CoT, which appends ``Let's think step by step'' to elicit intermediate reasoning kojima2022large , and our evidence-first CoT. This control distinguishes gains attributable to generic, longer reasoning from those obtained by explicitly grounding the decision in local visual evidence. All three variants use the same samples and require a final option letter for automatic matching. Table~ tab:api_models shows that the same training-free method can also be applied to commercial MLLMs, where Grok-4.20 obtains a clear overall improvement. Table~ tab:cot_control further isolates the effect of prompt structure on the three locally deployed open-source models. ZS-CoT raises InternVL3.5-8B from 42.47 to 44.31 and Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 43.13 to 43.57, whereas evidence-first CoT reaches 46.62 and 44.56, respectively. Thus, unconstrained step-by-step reasoning provides only part of the gain; explicitly verifying visual evidence is more effective overall. The direct-answer results show that current MLLMs still struggle with UMBench. title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
